---
title: The Agent Loop
description: Inside one KOD engine round — classification, grounding, streaming, tool rounds, steering, cancellation, and the round cap.
sidebar:
  order: 2
type: explanation
---

import { Aside, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Everything KOD does funnels through one loop: the engine takes an input, builds a grounded prompt, streams a response, executes any tool calls, feeds results back, and repeats. Understanding this loop makes the rest of the system legible: policy decisions, memory writes, skill matching, and session logging all hang off specific steps in it.

## One round, step by step

1. **Classify.** The [Task Router](/concepts/router/) reads the prompt and assigns a task type (`Simple`, `CodeModification`, `Debugging`, `Research`, …). The classification shapes the prompt and how many skills ride along.

2. **Ground.** The engine builds the grounded prompt from five ingredients, in a deterministic order:
   - identity (who the agent is and how it behaves),
   - environment (platform, working directory),
   - the [repository map](#the-repository-map),
   - matched [skills](/guides/skills/),
   - history plus [memory](/guides/memory/).

3. **Stream.** The provider streams tokens over SSE. Chunks reach the UI live — the TUI renders as the model speaks, not after. Tool calls are assembled from `ToolCallStart` / `ToolCallDelta` framing as they arrive.

4. **Gate and run tools.** Each tool call passes the [policy engine](/guides/policy/) first (allow/deny/ask, with the decision logged). Allowed calls execute under a timeout with per-path locks; mutating calls take a checkpoint first. An `ask` decision opens the approval dialog — and if nobody answers within 120 seconds, the call is denied rather than left hanging.

5. **Feed back.** Tool results become new context for the next model call. The loop returns to step 3 — stream again with the tool results in view — until the model answers without calling tools or the round cap is hit.

## The round cap

The loop runs at most **40 tool rounds** per prompt before the engine forces a wrap-up: one final call asks the model to summarise what was done and what remains. A typical non-trivial task uses 3–15 rounds, so 40 is a generous margin that still catches a runaway loop (a small model endlessly re-reading the same file) before you have waited minutes for nothing. The cap is fixed, not configurable — it is one of the few places KOD chooses a hard limit over unbounded adaptivity, and it is the reason a `kod agent` run always exits.

The `/goal` loop is separately capped at **6 turns** before it stops and reports progress, which you can refine with `/goal` or `/steer`.

## Steering and cancellation

Two controls make the loop interruptible mid-flight:

- **Steering** — typing a plain prompt while a generation runs queues guidance for the model without discarding completed work. In the TUI this is identical to `/steer`; in `kod chat` it works the same way. Steer notes are applied between rounds, at a safe boundary.
- **Cancellation** — `Esc` (TUI, normal mode) or `/cancel` stops the round. Completed tool results remain in the session, and the transcript records that the round was cut short.

One fixed concurrency detail matters here: the engine does not hold the provider read lock across the streaming round, which is why `/model` switches are instantaneous even mid-prompt.

## The repository map

Grounding includes a compact repository map — the same map `kod map` prints. It is how the model knows what exists in your project without reading every file: directories, key files, and top-level symbols. When routing or grounding surprises you, printing the map is the first diagnostic step; a map that misses a directory explains a lot.

## What the loop does *not* do

The loop is deliberately not a planner. It does not decompose goals (that is the [swarm runner's](/guides/swarm/) job), does not persist semantic memory (that is the memory manager's), and does not invent tool results — a refused tool call comes back to the model as a refusal, which is part of why policy denials change model behaviour rather than just failing silently.

<Aside type="tip">
  Watching the loop breathe: <code>kod chat --verbose</code> or the TUI's expanded tool rows (<code>t</code>) show each round's classification, matched skills, and tool calls in order. It is the fastest way to build an intuition for grounding.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Reference: Tools Reference" href="/reference/tools/" description="What the loop can call, and what each call returns." />

---
title: Architecture
description: How KOD is organised — the components behind the interface, the data flow through the engine, and the design principles behind it.
sidebar:
  order: 1
type: explanation
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';


> **Primary crate:** [`kod-core`](/reference/crates/#engine). Sub-crates: [`kod-core-routing`](/reference/crates/#engine), [`kod-core-state`](/reference/crates/#engine), [`kod-core-serve`](/reference/crates/#engine), [`kod-core-quality`](/reference/crates/#engine), [`kod-core-tools`](/reference/crates/#engine). See [Core crates](/concepts/core-crates/).

KOD is a multi-crate Rust workspace where each crate has a single responsibility and a narrow public API, so each part can be built and reasoned about in isolation. Twenty-six crates stack into four layers:

<Code lang="text" code={`┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CLI / TUI                         │
│           (kod-cli, kod-tui)                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                   Core Engine                        │
│                      (kod-core)                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                LLM Providers                         │
│        (kod-provider, kod-provider-openai)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                   Foundation                         │
│        (kod-types, kod-error, kod-config)            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘`} />

## The twenty-six crates

| Crate | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `kod-types` | Shared types: strongly-typed IDs (`AgentId`, `MessageId`, `SkillId`, …), messages, skills, memory, tools. |
| `kod-error` | `KodError` enum and `Result` alias — comprehensive errors with recovery detection. |
| `kod-config` | Configuration parsing and validation: endpoints, routing, memory, skills, swarm, hooks, MCP, and the policy engine's config side. |
| `kod-provider` | The `LlmProvider` trait, `GenerationOptions`, and streaming chunk types. |
| `kod-provider-openai` | OpenAI-compatible implementation (backed by `adk-model`): one code path for Ollama, LM Studio, MLX, vLLM, OpenAI. |
| `kod-skills` | Skill parser, loader, matcher, and hot-reload watcher. |
| `kod-memory` | Short-term memory and long-term `redb` storage, plus the context builder. |
| `kod-tools` | `Tool` trait, registry, the 24 built-in tools, per-path lock table, sandbox invocation. |
| `kod-swarm` | Agent lifecycle, communication hub, task coordinator, shared workspace. |
| `kod-core` | `KodEngine`, `TaskRouter`, `SwarmRunner`, repository map, session log, hooks, LSP and MCP integration. |
| `kod-tui` | Terminal UI: app state, event handling, widgets, keybindings, themes. |
| `kod-cli` | The `kod` binary: command definitions and handlers. |

The layering is strict: interfaces depend on core, core depends on providers and the domain crates, and everything sits on the foundation. No crate reaches sideways past the layer below it.

## Data flow through one round

<Code lang="text" code={`user input
   │
   ▼
┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
│  TaskRouter    │──▶│  Memory +      │──▶│  Grounded      │
│  (classify)    │   │  Skill match   │   │  prompt        │
└────────────────┘   └────────────────┘   └────────────────┘
                                                │
                                                ▼
┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
│  Tool results  │◀──│  LLM provider  │──▶│  Streaming     │
│  fed back      │   │  (streaming)   │   │  chunks → UI   │
└────────────────┘   └────────────────┘   └────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
│  Final reply   │──▶│  Session log   │
│  → CLI / TUI   │   │  (JSONL)       │
└────────────────┘   └────────────────┘`} />

1. **User input** arrives from the CLI or TUI.
2. **Task classification** (`kod-core::router`) decides the task type and how the round is shaped.
3. **Context building** (`kod-memory`, `kod-skills`) assembles memory entries and matched skills.
4. **LLM generation** (`kod-provider-*`) streams tokens and assembles tool calls live.
5. **Tool execution** (`kod-tools`) runs policy-gated calls and feeds results back.
6. **Response** reaches the interface while the **session log** records everything.

## Design principles

1. **Modularity** — each crate has a single responsibility and a narrow public API.
2. **Performance** — zero-copy parsing, object pooling, caching, connection reuse.
3. **Extensibility** — trait-based abstractions for providers and tools; MCP servers plug in from config.
4. **Type safety** — strongly-typed IDs prevent mixing an `AgentId` with a `SessionId`.
5. **Error handling** — comprehensive error types with recovery detection.
6. **Fail loudly** — corrupt configs warn and recover, missing sandbox primitives abort, absent providers refuse instead of inventing answers.
7. **Documentation** — every component documented; docs describe the code as it is.

## Performance posture

The workspace is deliberate about resource use: Tokio-based async I/O throughout, multi-level caching for skills and memory, object pooling and string interning to keep allocations down, and HTTP connection reuse for the provider. None of it is exotic — it is the accumulation of choosing allocations carefully in a program that streams tokens while running tools.

## What is deliberately not here

The in-repo `docs/SPEC.md` describes a larger aspirational system — a debugger integration, a full plugin API. Those are design references, not built features. LSP integration, MCP servers, and vector-based semantic memory, by contrast, *are* built and documented on this site. The architecture above is the system as it exists.

<Aside type="note">
  The [README's Project Status](https://github.com/elcoosp/kod#project-status) section is the authoritative list of what works end-to-end versus what is on the roadmap; this site follows it.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Concepts: The Agent Loop" href="/concepts/agent-loop/" description="What happens inside one engine round, step by step." />

## See also

- [Crates reference](/reference/crates/) — full index of all 26 workspace crates
- [Core crates](/concepts/core-crates/) — how the engine's internal sub-crates fit together
- [Agent loop](/concepts/agent-loop/) — the turn lifecycle
- [Compaction](/concepts/compaction/) — context reduction across turns

---
title: Citation Checks
description: When a reply cites a file and line, the engine verifies the location exists and annotates the ones that do not.
sidebar:
  order: 7
type: explanation
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A research answer that says "the bug is in `parser.rs:42`" is only useful if line 42 exists. Models hallucinate line numbers, and the cheapest correction is a deterministic pass that reads the cited location and reports what it found.

## What is checked

Two things, both local — no model call, no network:

1. the cited path resolves and is a file
2. the cited line number is within that file's line count

A citation passes only when both hold. One that fails either is annotated with `⚠` and the reason.

## What is deliberately not checked

A "does the cited line contain a word from the surrounding prose" heuristic sounds attractive and is not implemented. A false `⚠` on a correct citation is worse than no annotation at all: a user who sees the marker on a good citation learns to ignore it. The pass reports only what it can prove — the location exists, or it does not.

## Where it runs

Citation checking applies to **Research** task-type replies only. A coding turn never pays for it.

There are two passes, and the second is optional:

1. **Syntactic** — always runs. The two checks above, purely local.
2. **Semantic** — runs only when a Jev endpoint is configured. It asks whether the cited line actually supports the prose, which is the stronger claim. It is fail-open: a Jev error returns the reply unchanged and logs at heuristic level. A reply with more than ten citations has only the first ten checked — a hundred-citation reply is pathological, and the cap keeps the turn bounded.

## When you see the block

A reply with no citations, or with every citation verified, comes back clean. The annotation block appears only when at least one citation could not be verified, so a healthy session never sees it.

<Aside type="note">
  The pass never edits the reply. It appends a verification block listing what it found, so the original claim stays readable next to its verdict. On the streaming path the block is emitted as a chunk, which is why it appears as part of the reply rather than as a separate message.
</Aside>

## Why line numbers, not content

Line numbers are cheap to check and impossible to check by accident: either the file has 42 lines or it does not. Content matching would need to know what the model *meant* to cite, which is the hallucination being checked for.


---

---
title: Compaction
description: When a session runs out of context window, and what actually gets removed.
sidebar:
  order: 10
type: explanation
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Compaction shrinks a transcript so the next turn fits in the model's context window. `/compact` triggers it; the engine also runs it after a turn when the window is nearly full.

## When it fires

`used_tokens + reserve > window_tokens`, where `reserve = max(15% of window, 16_384)`.

A 200k window reserves 30k, so compaction starts around 170k used. A zero window never compacts — refusing is the safe reading when the window is unknown, and the caller learns the real number on the next provider call.

`/context` shows the live breakdown; the status line's context meter is the same number.

## What actually runs

Compaction is a preference list with fail-over, not a hardcoded ladder. The dispatcher holds an ordered set of methods and asks each whether it can reduce the context; the first that produces a non-empty plan wins.

The engine installs **three** methods, in this order:

| Order | Method | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `shake` (aggressive) | replaces large byte ranges inside tool results with a placeholder |
| 2 | `prune` | drops whole messages a later message supersedes |
| 3 | `handoff` | an LLM-written handoff document, when neither mechanical rung reduces enough |

The ordering is deliberate. The engine's dispatcher fires only *after* the threshold decision — the transcript is already too big, so the choice is "reduce now, or pay for a summary call". Under that pressure a cheap mechanical elision that clears the threshold beats an expensive LLM call. So the mechanical rungs go first and `handoff` catches what they cannot.

`shake` runs in its **aggressive** configuration here (protect 4,000 tokens, savings gate 0) rather than the default one. The default config assumes an opportunistic call on an otherwise-clean session, where "no reduction" is a fine outcome; under the engine's threshold regime, no reduction means a round-trip to the summariser.

The dispatcher's `default_ladder()` — `remote`, `snapcompact`, `handoff`, `shake`, `soft` — is the design's ordering for a deliberate compaction, not what the engine installs. Two of its five methods are stubs returning "unavailable": `remote` (provider-native compaction) and `soft` (local-LLM summary). `shake`, `snapcompact` and `handoff` are all implemented — `snapcompact` rasterizes the older half of the transcript into PNG frames for a vision provider.

## What `/compact` does

`/compact` is a **separate path** from the automatic threshold compaction above. It does not run the dispatcher ladder at all.

It keeps the last 20 turns and replaces everything before them with a summary message, pinned so the render path cannot drop it for budget reasons. The summary is the same factual `emergency_summary` the hard-threshold path falls back to — message count, tools used, file paths — with no attempt to explain intent.

<Aside type="note">
  Before this was fixed, `/compact` silently truncated: the dropped turns left nothing behind, so file paths, decisions and facts from them vanished from the model's view entirely. The automatic path had always summarised, so the two paths doing the same job had different consequences.
</Aside>

A summary is deliberately factual rather than an LLM-written recap: it runs synchronously, and a model call there would make an interactive command wait on the network. If you want the transcript summarised by the model, let the automatic path run — its `handoff` rung does exactly that.

## Shake in practice

Shake replaces large byte ranges inside tool results with a placeholder, keeping the message and its metadata. A 40 KB `read_file` result becomes a short line saying how many bytes were elided.

Two guards stop it destroying things it should not touch:

- **`protect_tokens`** (16,000 by default) — recent context is left alone even when large, because the model is probably still working with it. Shake's default is lower than prune's, since shake's mutations are smaller and more scattered.
- **`cache_warm_suffix_tokens`** (8,000 by default) — a suffix inside the provider's warm cache is not touched. Invalidating it would cost more than the tokens saved.
- **A whole-plan savings gate** — a pass that frees fewer than a threshold number of tokens is skipped outright, because the cache churn is not worth it.

Per-turn protected paths (files the turn is actively touching) are merged into the method's own config, so a file being edited is not shaken mid-turn.

## Plans, not mutations

Every method returns a *plan* — a description of the mutations — not a mutated transcript. The caller applies it. That keeps the methods pure and testable without an engine, and it means a plan can be rejected before anything changes: a plan that does not actually shrink the transcript is refused.

---
title: Core crates
description: How the engine's internal sub-crates (kod-core-*) fit together.
sidebar:
  order: 11
type: explanation
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The engine is not one crate. It is a family of six under `crates/kod-core*`,
organised so that each subsystem can be tested without spinning up the
whole engine:

| Crate | Owns |
|---|---|
| `kod-core` | The engine itself: `KodEngine`, agent loop, transcript, compaction dispatch, telemetry wiring, Jev advisor, swarm runner. |
| `kod-core-routing` | Task classification, context assembly, and model selection. Given a prompt and session state, it decides which provider/model to call and what context to send. |
| `kod-core-state` | Session persistence (`kod-state.redb`), file-level checkpoints, cost tracking, sensitivity classification. |
| `kod-core-serve` | ACP (Agent Client Protocol) JSON-RPC server for editor integration. Uses `tokio::sync::mpsc` channels to bridge the engine and connected clients. |
| `kod-core-quality` | `snapcompact` (context compression via inline PNG), `shake` (mechanical compaction — a deterministic last-resort reduction pass), `repomap` (tree-sitter symbol index generation). |
| `kod-core-tools` | The tool loop internals: dispatch guards, hook denial, fixtures, `execute_tool` orchestration. |

## Dependency direction

`kod-core` depends on all five sub-crates. The reverse is not true — the
sub-crates only see the traits they need. That keeps the compiler's
incremental build fast (a change inside `kod-core-routing` doesn't
re-compile `kod-core-serve`) and lets each subsystem ship its own tests
without instantiating the full engine.

## When to reach for which

- Adding a **new provider** → `kod-provider` (trait) + a new
  `kod-provider-*` crate. The router decides when to use it.
- Adding a **new tool** → `kod-tools`, then register it in
  `kod-core-tools::register_default_tools`.
- Adding a **new compaction strategy** → `kod-core-quality`, then wire
  it into `kod-core`'s `compaction_dispatcher`.
- Adding a **new storage backend** → `kod-core-state`.
- Adding a **new editor transport** → `kod-core-serve` or a new sibling.

## See also

- [Crates reference](/reference/crates/) — full index of all 26 workspace crates
- [Architecture](/concepts/architecture/) — high-level system diagram
- [Agent loop](/concepts/agent-loop/) — the turn lifecycle
- [Compaction](/concepts/compaction/) — how context shrinks across turns

---
title: Internal URLs
description: The four schemes read_file and write_file dispatch on — artifact, memory, xd, conflict — and what each one gives the model.
sidebar:
  order: 5
type: explanation
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

`read_file` and `write_file` do not only touch the filesystem. A path whose leading component is a registered scheme is handed to a protocol handler instead, which answers with a resource, a schema, or a side effect. This is how the engine lets the model reach things that are not files without spending a tool schema on each one.

| Scheme | What it reaches | Written by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `artifact://<id>` | raw tool output the minimizer replaced | the engine, after a minimize |
| `memory://<path>` | long-term memory entries | the memory tools |
| `xd://` | lazily-mounted tool schemas | `tool_search` / `batch` |
| `conflict://<id>` | one block of a merge conflict | the engine, when a file has markers |

## `artifact://`

When the [minimizer](/concepts/output-minimization/) rewrites a large tool result into something shorter, the original is stored and referenced by an `artifact://<id>` URL in the result JSON. Reading that URL returns the untouched capture — the model can ask for it deliberately, and a human can fetch it from the session log.

This is the difference between *truncating* and *minimising*: a 16 KiB cap throws away the tail, while an artifact keeps it reachable at the cost of one read.

## `memory://`

`memory://` delegates to the long-term store. Reading it returns entries that match the path; when memory is disabled the handler answers with a clear "memory is disabled" error rather than an unknown-scheme one, which is more useful to the model than silence.

## `xd://`

Lazy tool mounting. A tool marked `Discoverable` is removed from the provider's tools array, so its schema costs no prompt budget on every request. It stays reachable through this scheme:

- `read xd://` — list every discoverable tool by name
- `read xd://<tool>` — that tool's full schema and description
- `write xd://<tool>` — run it, with the JSON body as arguments

A schema-mismatch error returns the schema again, so a malformed call self-corrects in one turn without a second round trip. `tool_search` and `batch` are registered this way.

<Aside type="note">
  The scheme exists instead of a bespoke search tool because `read` and `write` are already in the tools array. A dedicated tool would cost a schema of its own and teach the model a second vocabulary for the same operation.
</Aside>

## `conflict://`

Resolving a merge conflict by reading the file and rewriting the whole thing is wasteful and easy to get wrong. When a file carries conflict markers, the engine scans them and gives each block a **stable id**.

- `read conflict://<path>` — scan that file and list its blocks
- `read conflict://<id>` — one block, with both sides and the labels
- `write conflict://<id>` — splice the final text into that block; the markers are removed

The model edits the block it cares about and nothing else.


---

---
title: Minimized Tool Output
description: How large command output is rewritten into something the model can use, and how the raw form stays reachable.
sidebar:
  order: 6
type: explanation
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';


> **Crate:** [`kod-minimize`](/reference/crates/#capability) — head/tail truncation, structured summarisation, `git diff` minimization.

A large tool result gets **minimised**, not truncated.

The difference matters. A cap chops at a byte boundary, and the part the model needed is very often the part that got cut: a verbose `pytest` run, a `cargo check` with fifty warnings, a `git status` on a big tree. A minimiser rewrites the output into a shorter form that keeps the informative content — a `git status` becomes branch plus file list, a `git log` becomes short hash plus subjects, a failing `cargo check` becomes the error slice.

## What it applies to

Each definition names a program and the subcommands it handles:

| Program | Forms |
| --- | --- |
| `git` | `status`, `log` |
| `cargo` | `check` (text and JSON), `test` |
| `pytest` | run output |

Anything else — a program with no definition, an unparsed shape — returns the raw capture unchanged. The minimiser never guesses.

## Pipes are opaque

`git status | grep modified` produces output that depends on the *next* stage of the pipeline. Rewriting it would misrepresent what the shell actually produced, so a command containing a top-level `|` is left alone entirely.

The same applies to `&&` and `;` chains: they are classified as a chain and returned raw, not minimised segment by segment.

## The raw output is kept

A minimised result carries an [`artifact://<id>`](/concepts/internal-urls/) URL for the original capture. Nothing is lost — the model can read the raw form deliberately when the summary is not enough, and a human can fetch it from the session log.

<Aside type="tip">
  If a minimised result is confusing, read the artifact. The summary is chosen by a fixed pipeline, not by the model, so it occasionally keeps the wrong half.
</Aside>

## When a definition does not apply

A definition can be restricted to a particular exit code — a `cargo check` definition that only fires on failure, for example — so a successful run keeps its full output. If a pipeline stage fails while minimising, the raw capture is returned and the failure is logged; a broken definition degrades to "no minimisation" rather than to a mangled result.

## ANSI stripping

ANSI escape sequences are stripped from command output before it reaches the model, whether or not a definition matched — a `cargo test` run with colour codes is cleaned even when its shape is unrecognised. This is on by default and not exposed as a config key; the built-in definitions also declare their own strip stage so a pipeline sees clean text throughout.


---

---
title: LLM Providers
description: KOD's provider layer — endpoints, the single OpenAI-compatible code path, base-URL normalisation, and streaming with live tool-call assembly.
sidebar:
  order: 4
type: explanation
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

KOD talks to models through one abstraction: the `LlmProvider` trait in `kod-provider`, implemented today by `kod-provider-openai` (backed by `adk-model`). The design bet is that almost every model server you might run locally — and OpenAI itself — speaks the same OpenAI chat-completions wire protocol, so one implementation covers all of them.

## One code path, many servers

All of these work unchanged, on the same code path:

<Tabs>
<TabItem label="Ollama (default)">
  <Code lang="toml" code={`[[llm.endpoints]]
name     = "local"
provider = "openai-compatible"
base_url = "http://localhost:11434/v1"
model    = "qwen2.5-coder:7b"
context_window = 32768`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="LM Studio">
  <Code lang="toml" code={`[[llm.endpoints]]
name     = "lmstudio"
provider = "openai-compatible"
base_url = "http://localhost:1234/v1"
model    = "your-model"
context_window = 16384`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="vLLM">
  <Code lang="toml" code={`[[llm.endpoints]]
name     = "vllm"
provider = "openai-compatible"
base_url = "http://localhost:8000/v1"
model    = "your-model"
context_window = 32768`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="OpenAI (cloud)">
  <Code lang="toml" code={`[[llm.endpoints]]
name     = "openai"
provider = "openai-compatible"   # "OpenAI" works too — same thing
base_url = "https://api.openai.com/v1"
model    = "gpt-4o-mini"
api_key_env = "OPENAI_API_KEY"   # the key lives in the environment
context_window = 128000`} />
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

The `provider` field accepts `openai-compatible` (aliases `Ollama` and `OpenAI`). The Anthropic provider is implemented and constructed by `build_provider`; see `crates/kod-provider-anthropic` for the wire format and `crates/kod-provider-anthropic/tests/contracts.rs` for the behavioural contract.

## Endpoints, not a single model

Endpoints are a list, and the first one is the default. Everything that affects the wire — `base_url`, `model`, `temperature`, `max_tokens`, `timeout_secs` — lives on the endpoint, which is what lets [routing](/guides/configuration/#endpoints-instead-of-a-single-model) send a swarm's planning to one server and its coding to another. API keys are referenced by environment-variable *name* (`api_key_env`), so a committed config cannot leak a secret, and optional `[llm.endpoints.pricing]` (USD per million tokens) feeds the TUI's cost display.

## Base-URL normalisation

Base URLs are normalised automatically: a server root (`http://localhost:11434`) or an `.../v1` root (`http://localhost:11434/v1`) both work. KOD composes the correct chat-completions endpoint either way, which removes the most common "connection works but requests 404" footgun when switching servers.

## Streaming and tool calls

Generation is streaming-first. The provider consumes SSE and emits chunks the UI renders live; tool calls get special treatment with `ToolCallStart` / `ToolCallDelta` framing, so a tool call is **assembled live as the model emits it** rather than buffered until the response completes. By the time the model finishes its turn, KOD already has the call ready to gate and execute — one reason the TUI's tool rows feel immediate.

Non-streaming generation exists too, but the engine's loop uses streaming everywhere, including inside [swarm](/guides/swarm/) agents.

## Model discovery

`kod models` calls the provider's `list_models()` (`GET /v1/models` upstream) with `--filter` to narrow the list. Errors are surfaced rather than collapsed into an empty list — a bad endpoint shows up as an error here instead of mysteriously showing "no models". The TUI's `/model` completion uses the same source, so the names it offers are the ones your server actually serves.

## What a provider must provide

The trait surface is deliberately small: generation (streaming and not) with tool calling, plus model listing. `GenerationOptions` carries temperature, token caps, and friends. That smallness is why the OpenAI-compatible path covers so many servers — and why a future second implementation (Anthropic's native protocol, for instance) has a clear shape to slot into.

<Aside type="note">
  Engine detail worth knowing: the agentic loop does not hold the provider read lock across a streaming round, so <code>/model</code> mid-prompt switches instantly — one endpoint's stream can wind down while the next spins up.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Guides: Model Profiles" href="/guides/profiles/" description="The four presets that make switching models a one-liner." />


---

---
title: The Repository Map
description: How the symbol map is built, what it skips, and why a thin map is usually a size cap rather than a bug.
sidebar:
  order: 9
type: explanation
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';


> **Crate:** [`kod-ast`](/reference/crates/#capability) — tree-sitter parsing for Rust, Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Ruby, Java, C.

The repo map is a compact list of top-level symbols per source file, built once and used to ground prompts. `kod map` prints it; the engine reads it when deciding what a change might touch.

## Building it

The walk honours `.gitignore` and skips the usual build trees, then extracts top-level symbols from each recognised file. Extraction goes through tree-sitter first and falls back to a regex scan when the grammar cannot produce a tree — the two paths emit the same `(kind, name, line)` tuples, so downstream code cannot tell them apart.

Nine languages are recognised: Rust, Python, TypeScript/TSX, JavaScript/JSX, Go, Ruby, Java, C and C++ headers. A file with any other extension is not scanned.

## Three things that make it stop

A map that quietly omits half your code is worse than no map, so each bound is deliberate and logged:

| Bound | Value | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Files per build | 100,000 | The walk is bounded by the workspace, and a workspace is bounded by nothing in particular. A monorepo with a checked-in `vendor/`, an ML repo with a dataset directory, or running from `$HOME` would otherwise scan until the disk fills. |
| Bytes per file | 2 MiB | A larger file is generated or vendored, not hand-written source. Skipping it costs nothing the model would use. |
| Symbols per file | 200 | A file with more than 200 top-level items is not a module a prompt can reason about. |

Hitting the file cap is **not an error**. The map is built from what fits and the truncation is logged, so a user surprised by a thin map can see why rather than guessing.

## Why a thin map usually is not a bug

In order of likelihood:

1. **The workspace is not detected as a code root.** Before scanning, the walk requires one of these in the directory: a VCS marker (`.git`, `.hg`, `.svn`, `.jj`) or a project manifest (`Cargo.toml`, `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`, `Gemfile`, `composer.json`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `Makefile`). A directory of loose scripts has none, and gets an empty map rather than a surprise walk of `$HOME`.
2. **The files are outside the recognised extensions.** A `.vue` or `.svelte` file is not scanned — those frameworks' component files are not in the extractor set.
3. **The files exceed 2 MiB.** Vendored bundles and generated sources land here.
4. **The 100k cap was hit.** The log says so explicitly.

<Aside type="tip">
  `kod map` prints what the engine actually sees. If it looks thin, check that first — it is the same data the prompt gets, not a summary of it.
</Aside>

## Rust is filtered

The Rust extractor drops functions marked `#[test]` or `#[tokio::test]`, matching the regex fallback's behaviour. A test module with fifty cases contributes one module symbol, not fifty — the production surface is what the map is for.


---

---
title: Task Router
description: How KOD classifies your prompt — the task types, how classification shapes grounding and skill matching, and how to steer it.
sidebar:
  order: 3
type: explanation
---

import { Aside, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The Task Router is the first thing your prompt meets. The router reads the input and assigns it a `TaskType`, and that classification quietly shapes the whole round: which skills are matched, how the grounded prompt is framed, and how the engine treats the result. It is keyword- and pattern-based — deterministic, fast, and inspectable — not a model call, which means classification costs nothing and never varies between runs of the same prompt.

## The task types

| `TaskType` | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| `Simple` | Questions, explanations, lookups — no code changes implied |
| `CodeModification` | Edits to existing code — refactors, doc comments, tweaks |
| `Debugging` | Failures, errors, misbehaviour to diagnose |
| `Research` | Exploration and understanding across many files |
| `Testing` | Writing or fixing tests |
| `Documentation` | Docs and comments as the primary output |
| `Complex` | Tasks that combine several of the above |
| `MultiStep` | Long-horizon tasks needing ordered operations |

## How classification affects the round

Two concrete effects worth knowing:

1. **Skill matching.** The router decides which skills ride along per prompt, up to `max_skills_per_query` (default 3) with a match threshold of `0.7`. A `Debugging` prompt and a `Documentation` prompt can surface different skill sets from the same directory.
2. **Prompt shaping.** The grounded prompt reflects the task type, so the model starts from a framing that fits the request instead of inferring one from scratch.

Classification also feeds [multi-model routing](/guides/configuration/#endpoints-instead-of-a-single-model): with `[llm.routing].by_task`, you can send `Debugging` work to a stronger endpoint while `Simple` questions stay on the fast local model.

## What the router considers

The router config carries the knobs that shape a round:

- `enable_memory` — whether memory participates in grounding.
- `max_skills_per_query` — the per-prompt skill cap.
- `working_dir` — the anchor for all relative paths in tool calls and globs.
- `context_window` — read from the endpoint; sizes the memory manager's per-prompt budget so long sessions do not drop entries that a large model could have kept.
- `short_term_capacity` — read from `memory.short_term_capacity`.

## When routing surprises you

Because classification is deterministic string matching, a surprising result is always traceable:

- `kod chat --verbose` (or the TUI's expanded tool rows) shows the classification for each round.
- The header in the TUI shows the task type as the round starts — `CodeModification`, `Debugging`, and so on.
- If a prompt is classified differently from what you intend, rephrase with the verbs the router keys on ("refactor", "debug", "explain", "write tests", "document") — or let `/goal` set a standing framing for the whole session.

<Aside type="caution">
  One deliberate design choice: the router used to return fabricated placeholder text when no provider was configured. It does not any more — a missing provider produces an explicit error instead of an invented answer. Fail loudly beats fake politely.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Concepts: The Agent Loop" href="/concepts/agent-loop/" description="Where classification sits inside the full round." />


---

---
title: Goals and Decisions
description: The two things a session remembers about itself — a budgeted objective, and the choices made along the way.
sidebar:
  order: 8
type: explanation
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A session keeps two kinds of durable state beyond the transcript: a **goal** with its own budget, and a **decision log**.

## Goals

One active objective per session, with a token budget and a wall-clock budget. The point is that a goal started ten turns in has its own accounting — "how much has *this* cost" is a different question from "how much has the session cost".

Cost is `(prompt_tokens − cache_read_tokens) + completion_tokens`, accumulated over the goal's lifetime. `cache_read` is subtracted because a token served from cache was already paid for by the write that put it there; counting it again would double-bill a long-running prefix. Tokens written *to* the cache are part of `prompt_tokens` and so are counted — a cache rotation can write a hundred thousand tokens that bill at the write rate, and a budget that ignored them would undercount exactly the long sessions it exists to bound.

When the accumulated cost crosses either budget, the status becomes `BudgetLimited` and one steer message is emitted — once, deduplicated — rather than continuing to spend quietly.

A goal still `Active` when the agent stops gets a hidden continuation message; one the user paused stays paused; a completed goal reports its final budget.

## Decisions

A running log of choices, so a later turn does not silently reverse an earlier one:

| Kind | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `user_preference` | "use tabs, not spaces" |
| `approach` | "use `similar` for the diff" |
| `file_change` | "add Tier 3.4 to the plan" |
| `constraint` | "do not add new deps" |
| `other` | anything flagged that fits none of the above |

Entries are per-transcript. A recent slice is rendered into the prompt, which is how the model sees a constraint stated twenty turns ago without the whole log being re-sent.

<Aside type="note">
  Neither is a substitute for the transcript. A goal bounds spend; a decision log keeps a stated preference visible. If something must survive both, it belongs in a skill or in long-term memory.
</Aside>


---

---
title: Contributing
description: How to contribute to KOD — the workspace conventions, what a good change looks like, the check suite your PR must pass, and how bug reports become fixes faster.
sidebar:
  order: 2
type: explanation
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Contributions, bug reports, and design discussions are welcome — KOD is a work in progress and says so up front. Contributions are licensed under MIT, the same terms as the project. This page condenses the repository's `CONTRIBUTING.md` into the practical loop: pick a scope, follow the crate conventions, pass the gates, open the PR.

## Find the right crate to touch

The workspace's modularity is your map. A change usually has one obvious home:

| You are changing… | Work in |
| --- | --- |
| Shared types, IDs, messages | `kod-types` |
| Error variants, recovery logic | `kod-error` |
| Config keys, validation, profiles, policy config | `kod-config` |
| Provider behaviour, endpoint handling | `kod-provider-openai` |
| Skill parsing, matching, hot reload | `kod-skills` |
| Memory eviction, storage, retrieval | `kod-memory` |
| A built-in tool, path locks, sandbox calls | `kod-tools` |
| Swarm coordination, workspace sharing | `kod-swarm` |
| The engine loop, router, repo map, session log, hooks, LSP/MCP wiring | `kod-core` |
| TUI behaviour, themes, keybindings | `kod-tui` |
| Command surface, doctor, completions | `kod-cli` |

Each crate has a single responsibility and a narrow public API — keep it that way. If a change seems to require reaching sideways across layers, that is a design smell worth raising in an issue first.

## The gates your PR must pass

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace
./scripts/test.sh      # the whole suite in one shot`} />

Clippy warnings are errors (`-D warnings`), and the `clippy.toml` encodes the project's lint preferences — run the linter before pushing, not in CI. Tests must pass offline; if you added a live-model test, gate it with `#[ignore]` and honour the `KOD_TEST_MODEL` / `KOD_TEST_DB` conventions (see [Testing](/developers/testing/)).

## Conventions that matter

- **Tests document behaviour.** New behaviour wants a test that pins it; bug fixes want a test that fails without the fix.
- **Fail loudly.** The codebase consistently prefers explicit errors over silent fallbacks — corrupt configs warn and recover, missing sandbox primitives abort, absent providers return `InvalidState`. Follow that grain.
- **Docs describe the code as it is.** Aspirational text belongs in issues or `docs/SPEC.md`, not in user-facing docs. When you change behaviour, the affected pages on this site want the same PR or a fast follow — every command flag and config key in these docs has been verified against the source once; keep it that way.
- **Changelog entries.** Notable changes get a bullet in `CHANGELOG.md` under the right section — the release notes are assembled from it, and the docs' changelog page mirrors it.

## Good bug reports

A report that includes the following gets fixed dramatically faster:

1. What you ran (the exact command) and what you expected.
2. What happened, with the relevant stderr/TUI output.
3. An excerpt of the session JSONL (it records every tool call *and* the policy decision that gated it).
4. `kod doctor` output (or `kod doctor --json`) — it answers the first five questions a maintainer would ask anyway.

## Where design happens

Big changes start as issues, not PRs. The repository keeps `docs/SPEC.md` as the design reference for the larger shape KOD could take, with `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` and `docs/TESTING.md` describing the code as it exists. If your idea touches the engine loop, policy, or swarm coordination, an issue first saves everyone a rewrite.

<Aside type="tip">
  The fastest credible first contribution is often a test: the suites are dense but small-grained, and a new case for an edge in <code>classify_task</code>, glob matching, or keybinding handling is both genuinely useful and a great way to learn the codebase.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Developers: Testing" href="/developers/testing/" description="The suite layout and the exact commands CI runs." />


---

---
title: Testing
description: How KOD is tested — the suite layout, offline-by-default design, live-model tests, benchmarks, and the pre-release checklist.
sidebar:
  order: 1
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The workspace's test suite runs unit tests, integration tests, and doc tests **without external services** — it is designed to be fast and offline, with live-model tests opt-in behind `#[ignore]`. `cargo test --workspace` is the single entry point; CI runs the same suite on every push.

## Quick start

<Code lang="bash" code={`just test                        # or:
cargo test --workspace           # all crates, all tests
cargo test --workspace -- --test-threads=8     # faster, parallel
cargo test --workspace --lib     # unit tests only
cargo test --workspace --tests   # integration tests only
cargo test --workspace -- --list | tail -1     # exact current total`} />

Per-crate, the dense suites are `kod-tui` (app state, events, keybindings, completion, search, streaming, main loop), `kod-core` (engine lifecycle, classification, memory wiring, grounding, tool rounds, session log, swarm runner), `kod-tools` (built-in tools, path resolution, sandbox invocation, permission enforcement), `kod-skills` (parser, loader, matcher, watcher, full pipeline), and `kod-memory` (FIFO eviction, `redb` round-trips, retrieval, compaction). `kod-provider` is trait-only and has no tests by design.

## Live model tests

Tests that exercise the real provider are `#[ignore]`-gated so `cargo test` stays fast and offline. Opt in with a running server and environment variables:

<Tabs>
<TabItem label="Provider tests">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`KOD_TEST_MODEL=qwen2.5:0.5b \\
  cargo test -p kod-provider-openai -- --ignored --nocapture`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="TUI main-loop test">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`KOD_TEST_MODEL=qwen2.5:0.5b KOD_TEST_DB=/tmp/kod-test.redb \\
  cargo test -p kod-tui --test main_loop -- --ignored --nocapture`} />
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

`KOD_TEST_MODEL` names a model the server has already pulled; `KOD_TEST_DB` points the TUI test at a disposable memory database. Connection errors here mean the server is down or the model is missing — not that the code is wrong.

In-process tests build the router with `enable_memory=false` to avoid database contention — mirroring how the engine wires memory in production but keeping tests hermetic.

## Benchmarks

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo bench --workspace          # or: just bench`} />

Benchmarks live under `kod-core/benches/` and cover the engine's hot paths.

## Debugging a failing test

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo test --workspace -- --nocapture              # full output
cargo test <name> -- --nocapture --test-threads=1  # serial, for races
cargo test <name> -- --backtrace                   # backtrace
cargo test -- --ignored                            # include live tests`} />

Common causes: Ollama not reachable (only affects `#[ignore]`-gated tests), permission errors in tool tests (path resolution assumptions), and TUI tests in CI (run serially where timing matters).

## Pre-release checklist

The full check suite — format + lint + test + release build — is scripted:

<Code lang="bash" code={`./scripts/test.sh`} />

Which mirrors the manual order: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`, then a release build. A `justfile` provides the shortcuts (`just build`, `just test`, `just lint`, `just check`, `just bench`).

<Aside type="note">
  CI (GitHub Actions) runs the same suite on every push and produces release artefacts via `release.yml`. Warnings are errors: the workspace builds clean with `-D warnings`.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Guides: Troubleshooting" href="/guides/troubleshooting/" description="What to do when the suite or a session misbehaves." />


---

---
title: Your First Session
description: A guided tour of the KOD TUI — modes, keybindings, slash commands, steering a running generation, and the context meter.
sidebar:
  order: 4
type: tutorial
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The TUI is where KOD is most itself: a header, a chat area with live tool rows, a status line, an input box, and a set of keybindings borrowed from the muscle memory you already have from Vim. This page walks through one realistic session from launch to exit and points out the parts that make the interface pleasant to live in.

## Launch and look around

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod tui`} />

The status line greets you with `Connected · <model> · N skill(s)` and reminds you that `/help` exists. If you have run KOD before, your previous conversation is restored automatically from `~/.kod/tui_session.json` — quit and reopen anytime, it keeps your place.

The interface has four regions. The **header** shows the session state and model. The **chat area** renders your prompts, the assistant's streaming replies, and one row per tool call. The **status line** carries the context meter and mode indicator. The **input box** is where prompts go, with history and completion support.

## Your first prompt

<Steps>
1. Press `i` to enter insert mode.
2. Type a goal that will make the agent use tools, for example:

   <Code lang="text" code={`explain the retry logic in src/net.rs and add a doc comment to the retry function`} />

3. Press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to send. Tokens stream in live; tool rows appear as the agent works.
</Steps>

Tool rows start collapsed: you see the tool name and target (for example `read_file src/net.rs ✓`). Press `t` to toggle tool-output visibility globally, `o` to expand the newest collapsed row, or `Enter` with the chat focused to expand the row under your cursor. This keeps the transcript readable while still making every call inspectable.

<Aside type="tip">
  The context meter in the status line shows how much of the model's context window the session is using. When it climbs past what you are comfortable with, <code>/compact</code> summarises the conversation to reclaim headroom, and <code>/context</code> shows a detailed breakdown of where the window is going.
</Aside>

## Steer a running generation

The single most useful thing to know: **typing a plain prompt while a generation is running steers it** — the same as issuing `/steer`. The input is queued, the model sees it as additional guidance, and the work already done is kept.

Use this when a run is heading the wrong direction and you would rather redirect than cancel. If you do want to stop, `Esc` (or `Ctrl-C`) cancels the running prompt.

## Slash commands worth trying first

Type `/` in insert mode to open completion — it also completes model names after `/model` and file paths. There are around fifty commands (the full list lives at [TUI Keybindings](/reference/tui-keys/)); a few worth trying in a first session:

- `/model <name>` — switch models mid-session. The switch is instantaneous because the engine does not hold the provider lock across a streaming round.
- `/goal <text>` — set a standing goal the agent works toward across turns (`/goal clear` removes it).
- `/attach <path>` — attach a file to your next prompt without waiting for the agent to find it.
- `/theme` — switch between the built-in `dark` and `light` themes.
- `/undo` — undo a `/clear`, in case you cleared more than you meant to.
- `/whoami` — one-line session summary: model, skills, context usage, paths.
- `/swarm` — launch a multi-agent run from inside the TUI.

Your own commands come free: a `[commands]` block in `config.toml` registers custom slash commands — see [Configuration](/guides/configuration/#custom-slash-commands).

## Keybindings at a glance

Normal mode (`Esc` leaves insert mode):

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `i` | enter insert mode |
| `Esc` / `Ctrl-C` | cancel the running prompt |
| `j` / `k` | scroll down / up (also arrows and mouse wheel) |
| `g` / `G`, `Home` / `End` | jump to oldest / newest |
| `PgUp` / `PgDn` | scroll by page |
| `t` | toggle tool-output visibility |
| `o` | expand the newest collapsed tool row |
| `f` | start a type-ahead search (`n` / `N` jump between matches) |
| `y` | copy the last assistant reply |
| `a` (or `Tab`) | open the agent panel |
| `e` | edit your last message |
| `u` | undo a `/clear` |
| `?` (or `h`) | help overlay |
| `q` | quit (asks for confirmation when a generation is running) |

Insert mode adds line editing: `Enter` sends, `Ctrl+J` (or `Shift+Enter`) inserts a newline, `Tab` cycles completions, `Up`/`Down` walk prompt history (your unsent draft is kept), `Ctrl+W` / `Ctrl+U` / `Ctrl+K` edit the line, and `Ctrl+Left` / `Ctrl+Right` jump by word. Every normal-mode key can be remapped — see [TUI Keybindings](/reference/tui-keys/#rebinding-keys).

## Exit cleanly

Press `q` in normal mode. If a generation is running, the TUI asks for confirmation rather than silently dropping the stream. Your session is saved under `~/.kod/` and can be inspected later with `kod sessions`:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod sessions show                          # where the session lives, message count
kod sessions export session.md             # write it out as Markdown (or --format json)`} />

<Aside type="note">
  Everything the TUI does is recorded: prompts, replies, and every tool call with its arguments and result. That is what makes <code>kod replay</code> possible — see [Sessions, Replay & Checkpoints](/guides/sessions/).
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Next: Scriptable CLI" href="/guides/cli/" description="The same agent loop, driven from scripts and one-shot commands." />


---

---
title: Installation
description: Prerequisites, building KOD from source, first-run setup with kod init and kod doctor, and shell completion installation.
sidebar:
  order: 2
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, Steps, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

KOD is distributed as a single Rust binary that you build from source. There is no package to download from a registry and no runtime to install: `cargo build --release` compiles the agent, the tools, the memory store, and the terminal UI into one executable at `./target/release/kod`.

## Prerequisites

Three things must be present on your machine before you build:

- **Rust 1.98.1 or newer**, installed via [rustup](https://rustup.rs/). The workspace uses the 2024 edition, so older toolchains will refuse to build it. The MSRV (`1.98.1`) is declared in `Cargo.toml` under `[workspace.package].rust-version`; `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the `stable` channel plus `rustfmt` and `clippy` components for reproducible tooling.
- **A model server** that speaks the OpenAI chat-completions protocol. [Ollama](https://ollama.ai/) is the recommended default and what the bundled profiles target first, but LM Studio, MLX Omni Serve, vLLM, and OpenAI itself all work unchanged.
- **Git**, required both for the built-in git tools (`git_status`, `git_diff`, `git_commit`, `git_branch`) and for `build.rs`, which stamps version information into the binary at compile time.

Two optional extras unlock more later: [bubblewrap](https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap) (`bwrap`) on Linux for `--sandbox`, and any [language server](/guides/tools/#write-follow-ups-lsp-and-check) on your `PATH` (rust-analyzer, typescript-language-server, …) for the LSP tools. Neither is required to start.

## Build from source

<Steps>
1. Clone the repository and build the workspace in release mode:

   <Code lang="bash" code={`git clone https://github.com/elcoosp/kod.git
cd kod
cargo build --release`} />

2. Confirm the binary landed and runs:

   <Code lang="bash" code={`./target/release/kod --version`} />

3. Optionally put it on your `PATH`:

   <Code lang="bash" code={`cp ./target/release/kod ~/.local/bin/   # or another directory on PATH`} />
</Steps>

The workspace builds on Linux, macOS, and Windows. A debug build (`cargo build`) is fine for trying things out, but the streaming tool loop is noticeably snappier in release mode.

## First run

KOD does not need any configuration to start — every setting has a sane default — but two commands exist specifically to make the first five minutes smooth.

### `kod doctor`

`kod doctor` prints a diagnostics report covering the configuration file, the model endpoint, discovered skills, the memory database, the sandbox primitive, and git. It is the fastest way to answer “is my setup actually working?” without launching a session, and it exits non-zero if any check fails — so you can also use it to gate a script:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod doctor            # human-readable report
kod doctor --json     # machine-readable, for scripts
kod doctor --fix      # create missing directories, write a default config`} />

`--fix` never modifies an existing config file; it only fills in what is missing.

### `kod init`

`kod init` prints where the config lives, the model profiles you can switch to, and the next three commands a new user should run. It is idempotent — running it twice changes nothing. With `--force` it rewrites the config from defaults (backing up the old one):

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod init
kod init --force      # reset to defaults, backing up the current file`} />

### Point KOD at a model

Model profiles bundle a model name, base URL, context window, and generation settings into a preset so a first-run user does not have to know what a `context_window` is. The built-in presets are `local-fast` (Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B), `local-capable` (32B), `local-reasoning` (DeepSeek-R1 14B), and `cloud-openai` (GPT-4o mini):

<Code lang="bash" code={`ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b    # one-time model download
kod profile use local-fast      # writes the preset into config.toml`} />

<Aside type="tip">
  Local profiles list their one-line install command (`ollama pull …`) right in `kod profile list`, so you can copy-paste without leaving the terminal.
</Aside>

### Start a session

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod tui`} />

The TUI opens, restores your previous session if you have one, and greets you with the loaded model and skill count. If you prefer a plain REPL, `kod chat` gives you the same agent in a scriptable shell.

## Shell completions

KOD can print a completion script for your shell, ready to source:

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="Bash">
    <Code lang="bash" code={`kod completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/kod`} />
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Zsh">
    <Code lang="bash" code={`kod completions zsh > ~/.zfunc/_kod`} />
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Fish">
    <Code lang="bash" code={`kod completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/kod.fish`} />
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Elvish / PowerShell">
    <Code lang="bash" code={`kod completions elvish
kod completions powershell`} />
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

## Keeping up to date

`kod update` checks GitHub for a newer release and prints the URL and install instructions. It is read-only — it never replaces your binary. To update, pull the latest source and rebuild with the same two commands you used to install.

<Aside type="note">
  Rebuilding after `git pull` is the intended upgrade path for now. Prebuilt release artefacts are produced by the CI pipeline, but the source build remains the canonical install.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Next: Quickstart" href="/getting-started/quickstart/" description="Your first chat, agent run, and replay in about five minutes." />


---

---
title: Quickstart
description: From zero to your first KOD chat, one-shot agent run, and session replay in about five minutes.
sidebar:
  order: 3
type: tutorial
---

import { Aside, Code, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This guide takes you from a built binary to a working agent session in about five minutes. By the end you will have chatted with a local model, run a one-shot agent against a goal, and replayed the tool calls it made — the three interactions that cover most day-to-day use of KOD.

If you have not built the binary yet, start with [Installation](/getting-started/installation/).

## 1. Make sure a model is running

<Steps>
1. Start the model server and download a small coding model:

   <Code lang="bash" code={`ollama serve &                       # start the server
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b        # small coding model, quick to pull`} />

2. Note the endpoint: the default config points at `http://localhost:11434/v1`, which is Ollama's OpenAI-compatible root. Base URLs are normalised automatically, so a server root or an `.../v1` root both work — the same is true for LM Studio, MLX Omni Serve, and vLLM.
</Steps>

<Aside type="tip">
  Don't want to pull a model right now? <code>kod profile use cloud-openai</code> targets OpenAI instead (requires <code>OPENAI_API_KEY</code> in the environment).
</Aside>

## 2. Verify the setup

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod doctor`} />

`doctor` checks the config file, the model endpoint, discovered skills, the memory database, the sandbox primitive, and git — and prints a one-line verdict for each. If anything is wrong, fix it here before moving on.

## 3. Switch to the fast local profile

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod profile use local-fast`} />

This writes the `local-fast` preset (Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B on `localhost:11434/v1`, 32k context) into your `config.toml`. You can see the effective `[llm]` block at any time with `kod profile show`.

## 4. Chat

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod chat`} />

This starts a plain REPL with streaming output. Type a question, watch tokens arrive, and exit with `Ctrl-C`. For the full interface — tool rows, agent panel, slash commands, search — launch `kod tui` instead.

For a single question without entering a REPL at all, use `kod prompt`:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod prompt "what does the retry function in src/net.rs do?"`} />

## 5. Run an agent against a goal

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod agent -g "add a doc comment to every public function in src/lib.rs"`} />

`kod agent` is a one-shot run: classify the task, build a grounded prompt, call tools, feed results back, and finish with a summary. It is the easiest way to see the tool loop work end-to-end. Add `--preset read-only` to watch it work without letting it write anything.

## 6. Replay what it did

Every session records its tool calls as JSONL under `~/.kod/sessions/`. `kod replay` re-executes those tool calls *without the model*, which turns any past session into a regression check:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod sessions latest                      # path of the newest session log
kod replay ~/.kod/sessions/<session>.jsonl --execute`} />

<Aside type="caution">
  <code>--execute</code> actually runs the recorded tool calls against your working tree. Drop the flag to print what <em>would</em> run — useful for reviewing a session before trusting it.
</Aside>

## Where to next

- [Your First Session](/getting-started/first-session/) — a guided tour of the TUI, including steering and slash commands.
- [Model Profiles](/guides/profiles/) — the four built-in presets and how to make your own.
- [Tools](/guides/tools/) — what the agent can do on your behalf, and how each call is gated.


---

---
title: Scriptable CLI
description: Driving KOD from the command line — prompt, run, serve, agent, swarm, replay, and the housekeeping commands, with practical recipes.
sidebar:
  order: 2
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The CLI is the scriptable half of KOD. It exposes the same engine as the TUI — the same policy engine, memory, skills, and session logging — through one-shot commands that compose well with pipes, cron jobs, and shell scripts. Where the TUI optimises for long interactive sessions, the CLI optimises for *repeatable* ones.

The full command surface is documented at [CLI Commands](/reference/cli/). This page is the practical tour.

## The shape of the binary

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod [--verbose] <COMMAND>`} />

Commands fall into five rough groups:

- **Sessions** — `chat` (plain REPL), `tui` (full interface), `agent` (one-shot goal), `prompt` / `run` (single prompt), `swarm` (multi-agent), `serve` (daemon).
- **Model management** — `models`, `profile`, `theme`, and the `[llm]` parts of `config`.
- **Inspection** — `skills`, `sessions`, `memory`, `map`, `doctor`, `config`, `tools`, `policy`, `sandbox`.
- **Audit and repair** — `replay`, `checkpoint`.
- **Setup** — `init`, `test`, `completions`, `update`.

Bare `kod` prints a short onboarding summary: the four entry points, where your config lives, and which skill directories were found.

## The four ways to send a prompt

**`kod chat`** starts a plain REPL with streaming output — the lightest way to interact with the model. No tool rows, no panel, just the conversation. Useful flags: `--model` to override the model for this session, `--system-prompt` to replace the built-in one, `--sandbox` to route shell commands through the platform sandbox, and `--preset` to override the policy for the session.

**`kod prompt "<text>"`** answers one prompt and exits — no banner, no REPL. The reply goes to stdout and diagnostics go to stderr, so it pipes cleanly. `-` reads the prompt from stdin. It is the command you want inside shell pipelines:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod prompt "summarise the TODO comments in src/ in a bullet list"
git diff main..feature | kod prompt -   # read the prompt from stdin`} />

**`kod run "<text>"`** is `prompt` in streaming form: the reply prints to stdout as it is generated instead of at the end. Same `-` stdin convention, same clean output.

**`kod agent -g "<goal>"`** runs a single agent against a goal — the full loop with tool calls — and exits when done. This is the workhorse for automation:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod agent -g "add a doc comment to every public function in src/lib.rs"
kod agent -n reviewer -g "summarise the changes in the last commit" --preset read-only`} />

<Aside type="caution">
  <code>kod agent</code> has no interactive consumer. When the policy says a write needs approval, the run refuses the write with an explanatory message rather than waiting — an unattended process cannot click <em>yes</em>. For scripts, either pass <code>--preset read-only</code>, accept the refusals by design, or use <code>--preset yolo</code> only where you truly mean it.
</Aside>

## The daemon: `kod serve`

Starting an engine per one-shot prompt costs process startup and engine init. `kod serve` starts a long-lived engine behind a Unix socket; `kod prompt --remote` sends prompts to it instead of building an in-process engine:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod serve &                        # daemon, listening on the default socket
kod prompt --remote "lint-check my last commit message"
kod serve --stop                   # ask the daemon to exit`} />

The socket lives at `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/kod.sock` (Linux) or `~/.kod/run/kod.sock` (macOS); `--socket <path>` overrides it. It is Unix-socket only, never TCP — there is no network surface.

## Inspecting the world

`kod skills` lists the merged skill set from every standard directory (or `--json` for scripts). `kod map` prints the repository map the engine uses for grounding — handy for sanity-checking what the agent can see (`--max-chars` caps the output, default 16000). `kod models` lists what the configured provider offers, with `--filter` to narrow. `kod tools list` prints the tool registry the model sees, `kod tools show write_file` one tool's schema, and `kod policy show` the effective permissions. `kod doctor` runs the diagnostics suite: config, endpoint, skills, memory, sandbox, git.

`kod config` is a small toolbox in itself:

<Tabs>
<TabItem label="Dump the effective config">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`# defaults merged with whatever you set — self-documenting
kod config show-merged`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Validate before use">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`# exits non-zero on invalid TOML — CI-friendly
kod config validate`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Edit, export, reset">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`kod config edit                     # $EDITOR
kod config export my-baseline.toml  # effective config to a file
kod config init-from local-fast     # backup + write from a profile`} />
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

## Auditing: replay and checkpoints

Two commands make KOD's audit story concrete:

<Code lang="bash" code={`# re-run every tool call from a past session — without the model
kod replay ~/.kod/sessions/1730000000000.jsonl --execute

# list file-level checkpoints, inspect one, restore it
kod checkpoint list
kod checkpoint diff <id>
kod checkpoint restore <id>`} />

`replay` is the regression check: any recorded session can be re-executed against the codebase at any later commit to see whether the same operations still make sense (or still pass). Without `--execute`, it prints what would run. `checkpoint` is the undo: KOD snapshots every file before a mutating tool call touches it, so `write_file` and `patch_file` damage is always recoverable — and `checkpoint diff` shows you exactly what restoring would change.

<Aside type="caution">
  <code>--execute</code> performs real writes and commands against your working tree. Review a session with plain <code>kod replay &lt;file&gt;</code> first when you are not sure what it contains.
</Aside>

## Recipes

A few patterns that work well in practice:

<Tabs>
<TabItem label="Nightly audit">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`# classify recent changes, read-only, no writes possible
kod agent --preset read-only \\
  -g "review yesterday's commits and flag risky patterns" \\
  | tee "$HOME/logs/kod-audit-$(date +%F).txt"`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Explain a diff in CI">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`git diff origin/main..HEAD | kod prompt - > /tmp/pr-summary.txt`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Long-running daemon for scripts">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`kod serve &
for f in $(git diff --name-only); do
  kod prompt --remote "review $f for obvious bugs" >> review.md
done
kod serve --stop`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Skill CI gate">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`# machine-readable skill inventory + validation for CI
kod skills --json
kod validate-skills`} />
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

<Aside type="tip">
  <code>--preset read-only</code> is the right default for any unattended run. It denies <code>write_file</code>, <code>patch_file</code>, and <code>execute_command</code> outright rather than asking — an unattended script cannot answer an approval prompt anyway.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Reference: CLI Commands" href="/reference/cli/" description="Every subcommand, flag, and default in one place." />


---

---
title: Configuration
description: How KOD reads config.toml — locations, every section ([llm] endpoints, [memory], [skills], [swarm], [tools], [hooks], [mcp], [commands]), clamping behaviour, and the config subcommands.
sidebar:
  order: 3
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

KOD reads its configuration from a single TOML file, auto-generated on first run, with sane defaults for every key. You can go from zero config to a working session without touching anything — the config exists so you can *stop* accepting defaults, not so you have to set them.

## Where the file lives

- **Linux:** `~/.config/kod/config.toml`
- **macOS:** `~/Library/Application Support/kod/config.toml`

`kod config path` prints the exact location; `kod config edit` opens it in `$EDITOR`; `kod config validate` parses it and exits non-zero when it is invalid — useful in CI or after a hand-edit. Corrupt files are not fatal: KOD warns and falls back to defaults instead of exiting, so a bad edit never bricks your session.

## The shape of the file

A config only needs the blocks you care about — every omitted section fills from defaults. The example below is a realistic *complete* file:

<Code lang="toml" code={`# ── Models ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[llm]
network_access = false          # opt-in network access for web_fetch

[[llm.endpoints]]               # one block per model server
name         = "local"
provider     = "openai-compatible"   # or "anthropic" (declared, not implemented yet)
base_url     = "http://localhost:11434/v1"
model        = "qwen2.5-coder:7b"
context_window = 32768
# api_key_env = "MY_API_KEY"    # env var NAME holding the key — never the key itself
# temperature = 0.7
# max_tokens  = 4096
# timeout_secs = 300
# [llm.endpoints.pricing]       # USD per million tokens, for TUI cost display
# input_per_mtok_usd = 0.15
# output_per_mtok_usd = 0.60

# ── Memory ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[memory]
short_term_capacity = 100
scope               = "global"  # or "project" → <cwd>/.kod/memory.redb
# extract_on_shutdown = false   # one LLM pass to save durable facts at exit

# ── Skills ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[skills]
enable_hot_reload     = true
max_skills_per_query  = 3
match_threshold       = 0.7
# skills_dir = "/custom/skills" # overrides the standard search paths

# ── Swarms ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[swarm]
max_agents         = 5          # clamped to 2–8 by the runner
merge_results      = true
agent_timeout_secs = 300        # per-agent wall clock; 0 disables
agent_retries      = 1

# ── Write follow-ups ───────────────────────────────────────────
[tools]
auto_check = false              # run compiler/linter after writes (cargo, tsc, ruff, go vet)
auto_lsp   = true               # run language-server diagnostics after writes

# ── Hooks ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[hooks]
enabled = false
# pre_tool_use  = { write_file = "rustfmt {path}" }
# post_tool_use = { write_file = "cargo check" }

# ── MCP servers (optional) ─────────────────────────────────────
# [mcp.servers.filesystem]
# command = "npx"
# args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/tmp"]
# enabled = true
# call_timeout_secs = 60
# [mcp.servers.filesystem.env]
# LOG_LEVEL = "info"

# ── Custom slash commands (optional) ───────────────────────────
# [commands]
# review = "Review the last change in {cwd} and point out risks."
# explain = "Explain what this code does:\\n\\n{args}"`} />

## Endpoints instead of a single model

The `[llm]` section holds a **list of named endpoints**, not one flat model. The first endpoint is the default; everything that affects the wire — `base_url`, `model`, `temperature`, `max_tokens` — lives on the endpoint. That is what lets you point different work at different servers:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[llm.routing]
by_task  = { Debugging = "cloud", Simple = "local" }
fallback = ["local", "cloud"]     # try in order when the primary fails
swarm    = { Planning = "cloud", Coding = "local" }`} />

- `by_task` maps a [task type](/concepts/router/) (`Simple`, `Debugging`, …) to an endpoint name.
- `fallback` is the ordered retry chain for retryable errors.
- `swarm` maps swarm capabilities (`Planning`, `Coding`, …) to endpoints, so a swarm can think with one model and code with another.

Names that do not match a defined endpoint are dropped with a warning at load time — a typo cannot silently disable a route.

## API keys live in the environment

Endpoint blocks never contain key material — only the *name* of the environment variable that holds it:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[[llm.endpoints]]
name        = "openai"
provider    = "openai-compatible"
base_url    = "https://api.openai.com/v1"
model       = "gpt-4o-mini"
api_key_env = "OPENAI_API_KEY"`} />

A shared or committed config therefore cannot leak a secret. The memory section has the same pattern for the optional embedding API (`memory.embedding_api_key_env`).

## Out-of-range values are clamped, not fatal

At load time every endpoint is validated: temperature is clamped to 0.0–2.0, `context_window` has a coherent floor (2000), `max_tokens = 0` falls back to the default, timeouts are floored at 1s, and empty `base_url`/`model` values are replaced. Each adjustment logs a warning naming the endpoint and the corrected value. The philosophy: be forgiving at load, loud about it, and precise once running.

## Per-project overrides: `.kod/`

Three things can be scoped to a project directory instead of your home directory:

1. **Policy** — `.kod/policy.toml` in the project root is committed to the repo like an `.editorconfig` and layers over your global config. See [Policy & Permissions](/guides/policy/).
2. **Memory** — `memory.scope = "project"` puts the long-term database under `<cwd>/.kod/memory.redb` instead of `~/.kod/data/kod.redb`, giving each project its own memory.
3. **Keybindings** — a `.kod-keys.toml` in the project remaps TUI keys for that repo only. See [TUI Keybindings](/reference/tui-keys/#rebinding-keys).

## Custom slash commands

The `[commands]` block registers your own TUI slash commands. Each key becomes `/key`, and its value is the prompt that gets sent:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[commands]
review  = "Review the last change in {cwd} and point out risks."
explain = "Explain what this code does:\\n\\n{args}"`} />

`{args}` is replaced by everything typed after the command name; `{cwd}` by the current working directory. `/review` needs no arguments; `/explain foo.bar` sends the template with `foo.bar` substituted in.

## Inspecting what actually applies

Because configuration comes from defaults plus your edits, the useful question is often “what is *effective*?” rather than “what did I write?”:

<Tabs>
<TabItem label="Effective config">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`kod config show-merged   # defaults merged with user config, reproducible`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Raw file">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`kod config show-raw      # verbatim file contents, comments included`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Just the LLM block">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`kod profile show         # the effective [llm] section`} />
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

`kod config export [path]` dumps the effective config to a file (or stdout with `-`; refuses to overwrite without `--force`), which gives you a fully self-documenting starting point.

<Aside type="tip">
  Piping <code>kod config show-merged</code> into a file and committing it is a clean way to version your baseline and diff future changes against it.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Reference: Config Reference" href="/reference/config/" description="Every key, type, default, and valid range in table form." />


---

---
title: FAQ
