description: Quick answers to the questions KOD users ask most — where data lives, how to reset things, why calls get blocked, and which command to use when.
sidebar:
  order: 14
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Short answers to the questions that come up most in practice. Each one links to the page with the full story.

## Where does KOD put its data?

Everything lives under your home directory — nothing is uploaded:

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Config | `~/.config/kod/config.toml` (Linux) · `~/Library/Application Support/kod/config.toml` (macOS) |
| Theme & keybindings | `theme.toml`, `tui_keys.toml` — same directory as the config |
| Skills | `~/.kod/skills/` and `~/.agents/skills/` (global) · `<project>/.kod/skills/` and `<project>/.agents/skills/` (project) |
| Long-term memory | `~/.kod/data/kod.redb` (global scope) · `<project>/.kod/memory.redb` (project scope) |
| Session logs (JSONL) | `~/.kod/sessions/<unix-ms>.jsonl` |
| TUI conversation state | `~/.kod/tui_session.json` |
| Prompt history | `~/.kod/tui_history.json` |
| Checkpoints | `~/.kod/checkpoints/<project-hash>/` |
| Daemon socket | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/kod.sock` · `~/.kod/run/kod.sock` (macOS) |

`kod config path`, `kod sessions show`, and `kod doctor` each print the relevant locations for your machine.

## How do I reset everything?

Per area, from safest to most destructive:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod sessions clear          # forget the TUI conversation
kod memory clear            # empty long-term memory (prompts; add --yes)
kod checkpoint clear        # drop this project's file snapshots
rm ~/.kod/tui_history.json  # clear prompt history
kod init --force            # rewrite config from defaults (backs up the old file)`} />

Deleting the memory `redb` file by hand works too — it is recreated empty on next use. `/clearall` in the TUI wipes chat, memory, *and* checkpoints behind one confirmation.

## Which command should I use — `chat`, `prompt`, `run`, or `agent`?

- `kod chat` — interactive REPL in your terminal.
- `kod tui` — the same, plus tool rows, panel, search, themes.
- `kod prompt "<text>"` — one question, one answer, clean stdout. Best for pipes and scripts. `-` reads the prompt from stdin.
- `kod run "<text>"` — same, but the answer streams to stdout as it is generated.
- `kod agent -g "<goal>"` — the full loop with tools: the agent may read, write, and run things until the goal is done.
- `kod swarm -g "<goal>" -n 4` — several agents on subtasks of one goal, merged at the end.

## Can I stop the agent from modifying anything?

Yes — three escalating ways:

1. `--preset read-only` on any run: `write_file`, `patch_file`, and `execute_command` are denied outright. 
2. A committed `.kod/policy.toml` with `forbidden` globs and `forbidden_binaries` — see [Policy](/guides/policy/).
3. Sandbox the shell: `--sandbox` confines `execute_command` with bwrap/sandbox-exec.

Check what would happen before running anything with `kod policy explain write_file path=src/main.rs`.

## Why did nothing happen when the agent tried to write?

Under the `standard` preset, writes and shell commands need approval. The TUI shows a dialog (`y`/`n`/Esc) and `kod chat` prompts on stdin. If nobody answers within 120 seconds — or the command has no way to ask, like `kod agent` — the call is denied. That is deliberate: an unanswered approval must not hang the loop, and unattended runs should ask nobody. Re-run with `--preset yolo` only where you accept unprompted writes.

## Why is my skill never matched?

Three usual suspects:

1. **Wrong directory.** `kod skills list` shows the merged set; if your file is missing, it is not in one of the four search paths (or `skills_dir` overrides them).
2. **Trigger overlap.** Matching scores triggers, tags, capabilities, and name against your prompt with a threshold (`match_threshold`, default 0.7). Run `kod skills search "<words from your prompt>"` — if your skill does not appear, its triggers share no words with how you actually ask.
3. **Broken front matter.** `kod validate-skills` parses every file and reports what fails; `kod skills show <name>` prints what KOD parsed (which may differ from what you wrote).

## How do I switch models mid-session?

`/model <name>` in the TUI — completion lists what your server actually offers. The switch is instant, even mid-generation. From the shell, `kod profile use <profile>` writes a preset into your config, or `--model` overrides per run. See [Model Profiles](/guides/profiles/).

## Can I use OpenAI? Anthropic? Gemini?

Any server that speaks the OpenAI chat-completions protocol works today: Ollama, LM Studio, MLX Omni Serve, vLLM, OpenAI itself. Point an `[[llm.endpoints]]` block at it and put the API key in an environment variable named by `api_key_env` — never in the file. An `anthropic` provider kind is recognised in config but not implemented yet; it fails at the first prompt, with a startup warning so the gap is visible early.

## How much context do I have left?

The status line's context meter in the TUI shows usage live; `/context` breaks it down, `/compact` summarises the conversation to reclaim headroom, and `/pin <n>` protects a message from compaction. The window size comes from `context_window` on your endpoint — set it to match your model (the built-in profiles do).

## What did the agent actually change?

- Tool rows in the TUI show a unified diff inline for every `write_file`/`patch_file` (`t` to expand).
- `/diff` shows the most recent file change; `/checkpoints` lists snapshots and `/rollback <id>` restores one.
- `git_status` / `git_diff` are the agent's own view — run them yourself before committing.

## Does KOD work on Windows?

The workspace builds on Windows and the agent runs, but shell sandboxing is unavailable there — `--sandbox` reports the primitive as missing and fails loudly. Sandboxed workflows are a Linux/macOS feature today.

## Where are the example skills?

The repository ships `code-review`, `python-testing`, and `rust-refactoring` under `skills/examples/` — copy one into `~/.kod/skills/` and edit. See [Skills](/guides/skills/).

<Aside type="tip">
  Still stuck? <code>kod doctor --json</code> output plus the newest session log answer most questions a maintainer would ask — see [Troubleshooting](/guides/troubleshooting/) for the full triage flow.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Guides: Troubleshooting" href="/guides/troubleshooting/" description="Symptom-first fixes for the common failures." />


---

---
title: Hooks
description: Running your own shell commands around tool calls — pre_tool_use and post_tool_use hooks driven by config templates.
sidebar:
  order: 12
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Hooks let you run your own shell commands at two points in the tool lifecycle: **before** a tool executes (`pre_tool_use`) and **after** it completes (`post_tool_use`). They are driven entirely by config templates — no scripting language to learn, no plugin API to import — which keeps them auditable like everything else in KOD: a hook is a line in your `config.toml`.

## Enabling hooks

<Code lang="toml" code={`[hooks]
enabled = false
# pre_tool_use  = { write_file = "rustfmt {path}" }
# post_tool_use = { write_file = "cargo check" }`} />

Hooks are disabled by default. Flipping `enabled = true` activates both maps. Each entry keys a **tool name** (`write_file`, `patch_file`, `execute_command`, …) to a **shell command template**, and `{path}`-style placeholders are substituted with the tool call's arguments before execution.

## What they are good for

The canonical pair from the config comments shows the intended shape:

- **`pre_tool_use` on `write_file`: `rustfmt {path}`** — every file the agent writes gets formatted the moment it lands, so style is enforced at the source rather than reviewed at the end.
- **`post_tool_use` on `write_file`: `cargo check`** — every write is immediately followed by a compile check, so a broken edit surfaces in the same round that produced it instead of five prompts later.

The same pattern extends naturally: run `eslint --fix` after JavaScript edits, `gofmt` after Go writes, or a quick test suite after any `patch_file` on a crate you care about.

<Aside type="tip">
  If all you want is post-write diagnostics, check whether the built-in switches do it first: <code>tools.auto_lsp = true</code> (default) appends language-server diagnostics after writes, and <code>tools.auto_check = true</code> runs the project compiler/linter with baseline-aware output. Hooks are for commands that are *yours* — formatters with house rules, notification bells, snapshot scripts.
</Aside>

## How hooks relate to policy

Hooks execute *inside* the tool lifecycle, not in place of it. The order per call is:

1. Policy decision (preset → global → project → CLI) — allow, deny, or ask.
2. If allowed: `pre_tool_use` hook for this tool, if one is configured.
3. The tool executes (sandboxed if requested, path-locked, checkpointed if mutating).
4. `post_tool_use` hook, if configured.

A denied tool call never reaches its hooks — there is nothing to hook around. Hook commands are themselves shell commands, so treat them with the same care as policy allowlists: they run with your permissions, outside the tool sandbox.

<Aside type="caution">
  Keep hooks fast. A <code>post_tool_use</code> hook runs after every matching tool call — a hook that takes 30 seconds turns every write into a 30-second round. <code>cargo check</code> is a good hook; <code>cargo test</code> usually is not.
</Aside>

## Where hooks live in the engine

The hook system lives in `kod-core` alongside the session log. Hook commands run in your session's shell with your privileges; their output is not injected into the model's prompt — if you want the model to *see* the result of a check, that is precisely what `tools.auto_check` and the `check` tool are for (see [Tools](/guides/tools/#write-follow-ups-lsp-and-check)).

<LinkCard title="Guides: Tools" href="/guides/tools/" description="The tool families hooks attach to." />


---

---
title: Language Server Integration
description: Which servers KOD looks for, how diagnostics reach the model, and what happens when none is installed.
sidebar:
  order: 13
type: how-to
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

KOD uses language servers for two things: the `lsp_*` tools the model calls explicitly, and a diagnostics pass that runs after a successful write so the model sees errors on its next turn without asking.

Nothing here is required. With no server on `PATH` the tools report a missing capability and the write path simply skips the pass.

## Which server, for which file

Detection is by extension, then a check that the binary is on `PATH`:

| Extension | Server, in order tried |
| --- | --- |
| `.rs` | `rust-analyzer` |
| `.py` | `pyright-langserver`, then `pylsp` |
| `.ts` `.tsx` `.js` `.jsx` | `typescript-language-server` |
| `.go` | `gopls` |

Anything else has no server. That is not an error — the tool reports which capability is missing rather than returning an empty result, so the model learns to fall back to the compiler-based `check` instead of concluding the file is clean.

## The four tools

| Tool | Answers |
| --- | --- |
| `lsp_diagnostics` | current diagnostics for a file |
| `lsp_definition` | where a symbol is defined |
| `lsp_references` | where a symbol is referenced |
| `lsp_hover` | the type and documentation at a position |

## Diagnostics after a write

With `[lsp] auto_diagnostics` on (the default), a successful write triggers a diagnostics pass on the touched file. It waits `settle_ms` (500 ms) for the server to publish, then appends a `## LSP diagnostics` block to the next turn's prompt.

A slow server on a large workspace can take seconds. Making the write wait all of that is the wrong trade, so a second background pass keeps watching with a longer budget — `deferred_settle_ms` (12 s). What it finds is queued and drained into the *next* turn's prompt under `## LSP diagnostics (late)`, which is where the errors matter anyway.

Two details keep the late queue honest:

- **Dedup.** A server republishes its whole list on every change, so an entry equal to one already queued for that transcript is dropped. Without it a busy rust-analyzer would queue the same thirty errors on every keystroke.
- **Version guard.** The background task records the file's mtime when spawned and only pushes a result if the file still has that mtime. A write during the wait makes the answer stale, and it is discarded rather than reported against content that no longer exists.

<Aside type="note">
  KOD has no LSP document version on the engine side, so mtime stands in for one. It is coarser — two writes inside the same filesystem timestamp tick would look identical — but it needs no coordination with the server.
</Aside>

## Tuning

| Key | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto_diagnostics` | `true` | Run the post-write pass at all |
| `settle_ms` | `500` | How long the inline pass waits |
| `deferred_enabled` | `true` | Run the late background pass |
| `deferred_settle_ms` | `12000` | How long that pass waits |

Two switches gate the pass, and **both** must be on: `[tools] auto_lsp` (true by default, the coarse on/off used by `kod doctor` and the TUI toggle) and `[lsp] auto_diagnostics` (true by default, the persistent config choice). Turning either off disables it. `kod doctor` names which one turned it off rather than reporting a generic "diagnostics disabled".


---

---
title: MCP Servers
description: Connect Model Context Protocol servers, how their tools are named and gated, and why startup is fast on the second run.
sidebar:
  order: 12
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

MCP servers extend the agent with tools it does not ship itself. Each server is a subprocess that speaks the Model Context Protocol; KOD spawns it at startup, asks what tools it has, and registers one adapter per tool.

## Configuring a server

One `[mcp.servers.<name>]` block per server. The name is the routing key.

<Code lang="toml" code={`[mcp.servers.filesystem]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/tmp"]
enabled = true
call_timeout_secs = 60

[mcp.servers.filesystem.env]
LOG_LEVEL = "info"`} />

| Key | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `command` | — | The program to spawn, resolved against `$PATH`. |
| `args` | `[]` | Arguments to it. |
| `env` | `{}` | Added to the child's environment. The child inherits yours, so a `PATH` you set in the shell reaches the server. |
| `enabled` | `true` | When false the block is configured but no process is spawned — useful for keeping a server's settings as a record. |
| `call_timeout_secs` | `60` | Per-`tools/call` timeout. `initialize` and `tools/list` use fixed client timeouts. |

A missing `[mcp]` section means no MCP tools, which is the default.

## How tools are named

A server named `filesystem` advertising `read_file` becomes **`mcp:filesystem.read_file`** in the model's tool inventory.

The dot is the separator, and the split is on the *first* dot after the `mcp:` prefix — so a server that names a tool `foo.bar` maps back correctly from `mcp:filesystem.foo.bar`. Tool names are verbatim from the server; only the prefix and the server name are KOD's.

## Gating

Every MCP adapter declares an all-false permission bitmask. That is deliberate: **the policy engine is the security boundary, not the bitmask.** Under the default `standard` preset MCP tools ask before running. To allow one:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[tools."mcp:filesystem.read_file"]
mode = "allow"`} />

Policy entries address the full name, including the `mcp:` prefix.

## Startup is cached

The first start of a server costs a process spawn plus a `tools/list` round trip. The result is cached under the platform cache directory (`kod/mcp/`), keyed on the command, arguments, and environment, with a **30-day** TTL. A second start reads the cache and registers the tools without spawning — which matters when several servers are configured.

A cache entry is deleted on read when stale, so a changed `args` or `env` produces a different key and a fresh list rather than a stale one.

<Aside type="caution">
  The cache means a server that *changes its tools without changing its command line* keeps the old list until the TTL expires. Bump an unused argument to invalidate it, or clear the cache directory.
</Aside>


---

---
title: Memory
description: How KOD's multi-layer memory works — short-term FIFO, long-term redb storage, global vs project scope, retrieval, and the kod memory commands.
sidebar:
  order: 6
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

KOD's memory system has two layers with one job each: **short-term** memory keeps the current session coherent, and **long-term** memory persists facts across sessions in a file you can inspect and delete. Both are local by default — the long-term store is a `redb` database under your home directory, not a cloud service.

## Short-term memory

Short-term memory is in-memory with a capacity limit (`memory.short_term_capacity`, default 100 entries). It behaves as a FIFO: new entries push old ones out once the buffer is full. The point is not archive — it is keeping the *current* conversation grounded so the model does not lose the thread halfway through a long session.

Capacity interacts with the model's context window. The engine reads `llm.endpoints[].context_window` and sizes the memory manager's per-prompt context budget accordingly, so a long-running session does not silently drop memory entries that would comfortably fit a large model.

## Long-term memory

Long-term memory is a persistent `redb` key-value database. Entries survive sessions, and retrieval uses keyword and recency scoring against your prompt: when you say something related to a stored fact, the fact rides along in the grounded prompt.

Where the database lives is controlled by `memory.scope`:

- `"global"` (default) — one database at `~/.kod/data/kod.redb`, shared by all projects.
- `"project"` — one database per project, at `<cwd>/.kod/memory.redb`, so work code and personal experiments never cross-contaminate.

Setting `memory.long_term_db_path` overrides both with an explicit location.

<Aside type="tip">
  Project scope is the least surprising choice for people who work across many repositories. Global scope is convenient when your notes are about tooling and workflows rather than specific codebases. Either way, the file is yours: open it, inspect it, delete it.
</Aside>

## Working with memory from the CLI and TUI

Memory is a first-class citizen of the command surface, not a black box:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod memory list                     # every long-term entry, newest first
kod memory search "rate limiter"    # case-insensitive substring search
kod memory delete <short-id>        # remove one entry (id from list/search)
kod memory export memories.json     # dump everything (or \`-\` for stdout)
kod memory import memories.json     # append entries; existing ones kept
kod memory clear                    # delete everything — prompts unless --yes`} />

Inside the TUI, `/memory` lists entries and supports the same operations: `/memory search <q>`, `/memory delete <id>`, `/memory clear`.

## What gets remembered

Two paths put facts into long-term memory:

1. **The agent itself.** The `memory_save` and `memory_search` tools are registered whenever memory is enabled — the model can decide to persist a durable fact ("user prefers `unwrap_or_else` over `unwrap` here") and look it up later, and you will see those calls as ordinary tool rows.
2. **Session extraction, on demand.** Setting `memory.extract_on_shutdown = true` runs one cheap LLM call when a session ends, pulling durable facts out of the transcript and storing up to `memory.extract_max_entries` (default 12) of them. It is off by default because it costs one LLM call per session.

The engine stores facts it deems durable — decisions, preferences, corrections you made (“we don't use camelCase here”) — rather than entire transcripts. Transcripts themselves live in the session log (see [Sessions, Replay & Checkpoints](/guides/sessions/)), which is a different mechanism with a different purpose: audit, not recall.

## Optional: semantic search

By default retrieval is keyword + recency — deterministic and free. KOD can additionally embed entries for semantic matching:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[memory]
enable_semantic_search = true
embedding_endpoint     = "ollama"   # or "openai"; "none" (default) disables
# embedding_url = "http://localhost:11434"   # derived from llm.base_url if unset
# embedding_api_key_env = "OPENAI_API_KEY"   # for the openai endpoint
# embedding_model = "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"`} />

`embedding_endpoint = "ollama"` uses Ollama's `/api/embed`, deriving the URL from your LLM `base_url` unless `embedding_url` is set. `openai` speaks `/v1/embeddings` with the key read from the named environment variable.

## Tuning

<Code lang="toml" code={`[memory]
short_term_capacity = 100        # FIFO entries kept per session
scope               = "global"   # or "project"
# long_term_db_path      = "/data/kod/memory.redb"  # explicit path
# compaction_interval_secs = 3600`} />

Practical guidance:

- **Raise `short_term_capacity`** for very long interactive sessions on models with big context windows; the engine will budget against `context_window` rather than evict early.
- **Prefer `scope = "project"`** when memory entries would otherwise leak between unrelated codebases.
- **A wrong entry beats a lost entry** in retrieval today — retrieval scores word overlap, so write stored facts the way you would search for them later.
- **Resetting is safe**: deleting the `redb` file (or `kod memory clear`) loses nothing but memory — config, sessions, and checkpoints are separate.

<Aside type="caution">
  Semantic search requires a running embedder at the configured endpoint. If you enable it and the endpoint is down, retrieval falls back to keyword matching — check <code>kod doctor</code> if entries stop resurfacing.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Reference: Config Reference" href="/reference/config/" description="Every memory key, its type, and its default." />


---

---
title: Policy & Permissions
description: The four-layer policy engine — presets, global config, project .kod/policy.toml, and CLI overrides — with per-tool allow/deny/ask, path globs, and command allowlists.
sidebar:
  order: 8
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A `Policy` says what the agent is allowed to do, project by project. It is read from `.kod/policy.toml` in the project root, merged over a preset, and consulted by the engine **before every tool call**. The decision replaces ad-hoc flags and scattered permission bitmasks: one engine, one decision point, one log entry per call.

## Four layers, later overriding earlier

1. **Preset** — `read-only`, `standard`, or `yolo`. The default preset is `standard`.
2. **Global config** — the `[tools]` and `[llm]` sections of your `config.toml` (network access defaults).
3. **Project policy** — `.kod/policy.toml`, committed to the repo like an `.editorconfig`.
4. **CLI override** — `--preset yolo` on the command line.

Within a layer, `[tools.<name>]` entries give a per-tool decision (`allow` / `deny` / `ask`) plus optional path globs and command allowlists. A `deny` always wins over an `allow` at glob-conflict time — the same rule `ToolContext::is_path_allowed` applies.

## The three presets

| Preset | Reads | Writes / shell | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `read-only` | allowed | **denied without asking** | unattended runs, code review, auditing |
| `standard` *(default)* | allowed | **require approval** | everyday interactive work |
| `yolo` | allowed | **allowed without prompting** | trusted throwaway sandboxes |

`standard` asks before writes and shell commands: an approval dialog in the TUI (`y`/`n`/Esc), a stdin prompt in `kod chat`. An unanswered approval times out after **120 seconds and defaults to deny** — a dialog nobody walks up to must not hang the tool loop forever.

`read-only` is the right default for any unattended script — a script cannot answer an approval prompt, so asking would be a lie. `yolo` exists for trusted throwaway sandboxes where the prompts cost more than they protect.

<Aside type="caution">
  <code>kod agent</code> and <code>kod prompt</code> have no interactive consumer: under <code>standard</code>, calls that need approval are refused immediately with a message the model and you can act on, rather than blocking. Design unattended runs around <code>--preset read-only</code> or an explicit project policy.
</Aside>

## Writing a `.kod/policy.toml`

<Code lang="toml" code={`# .kod/policy.toml — committed to the repo
preset = "standard"

[tools.write_file]
mode = "ask"
paths    = ["src/**", "docs/**"]
forbidden = ["**/.env", "**/*.pem"]

[tools.execute_command]
mode = "ask"
binaries           = ["cargo", "rustfmt", "git"]
forbidden_binaries = ["curl", "rm"]

[tools.web_fetch]
mode    = "allow"
network = true
domains = ["docs.rs", "crates.io"]

[git]
history_protected = true   # .git is mounted read-only at the sandbox`} />

Field reference:

- `mode` — overrides the preset's decision for this tool: `allow`, `deny`, or `ask`.
- `paths` — allow-list of path globs; a path matching none of them is denied.
- `forbidden` — forbidden path globs; deny wins over allow.
- `binaries` / `forbidden_binaries` — command allow/deny lists, meaningful for `execute_command`; a command whose first token is not allow-listed is denied. This is convenience, never a security guarantee — the sandbox is.
- `network` — per-tool override of the global `llm.network_access`.
- `domains` — domain allow-list for `web_fetch` when network is enabled.
- `git.history_protected` — mounts `.git` read-only at the sandbox (default true).

## Glob semantics

Path globs follow gitignore intuition, implemented with `globset` and `literal_separator(true)`: `*` does not cross `/`, `**` does. A pattern is tried three ways — verbatim (for absolute patterns), relative to the working directory (the usual project-relative form like `src/**`), and, unless the pattern is anchored, prefixed with `**/` so `src/**` also matches files under nested directories the way a shell glob would.

## Asking "why was it denied?" without a session

`kod policy show` prints the effective policy — the preset in force, every per-tool override, and which layer set each rule. `kod policy explain` answers the sharper question, *what would the engine decide for this exact call?*:

<Tabs>
<TabItem label="Show the policy">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`kod policy show`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Explain one call">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`kod policy explain write_file path=src/main.rs
kod policy explain execute_command command="cargo test"
kod policy explain web_fetch url=https://docs.rs/`} />
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

The verdict matches what a session would do: the project policy layer is loaded from the current directory, session-scoped deny rules (added at runtime, e.g. by a swarm) are not present in a fresh CLI process, and a `--preset` CLI override is *not* applied — the inspection shows the config's answer, not a hypothetical.

## Every decision is logged

`PolicyEngine::decide` is pure with respect to the tool call: it takes the tool name, the JSON arguments, and the effective `ToolContext` (whose `working_dir` anchors relative paths), and returns a `PolicyDecision { outcome, rule, source }`. The engine logs this as a `SessionEntry::PolicyDecision` and then runs, refuses, or asks. That means the JSONL session log answers *why* a call was allowed or refused, not just *what* happened — replay it, read it, or diff it.

<LinkCard title="Next: Sandboxing" href="/guides/sandboxing/" description="OS-level containment for shell commands — bwrap and sandbox-exec." />


---

---
title: Model Profiles
description: The built-in model profiles — local-fast, local-capable, local-reasoning, cloud-openai — and how to switch, inspect, and seed config from them.
sidebar:
  order: 4
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

First-run friction is the single easiest adoption problem to fix, and KOD fixes it with **model profiles**: named presets that bundle a model name, base URL, context window, and generation settings. Instead of learning what a `context_window` is, you run `kod profile use local-fast` and get a working session.

## The built-in presets

| Profile | Model | Context | Endpoint | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `local-fast` | `qwen2.5-coder:7b` | 32k | `http://localhost:11434/v1` | Small local model for quick edits and questions. The recommended starting point. |
| `local-capable` | `qwen2.5-coder:32b` | 32k | `http://localhost:11434/v1` | Larger local model for harder tasks — needs roughly 20 GB VRAM. |
| `local-reasoning` | `deepseek-r1:14b` | 64k | `http://localhost:11434/v1` | Reasoning-focused local model (DeepSeek-R1 14B). |
| `cloud-openai` | `gpt-4o-mini` | 128k | `https://api.openai.com/v1` | OpenAI cloud; requires `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the environment. |

Every local profile carries a one-line install command (`ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b`, and so on) so the model download is a copy-paste away from `kod profile list`.

## The `kod profile` commands

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod profile list             # show the built-in presets (add --json for scripts)
kod profile show             # print the effective [llm] config
kod profile use local-fast   # write the preset's values into config.toml
kod profile use local-capable --dry-run   # print what would be written`} />

`use` edits the first `[llm.endpoints]` block in your config file in place. With `--dry-run` it prints the changes without touching anything, which is useful when you want to copy values into a custom config rather than apply them.

<Aside type="tip">
  Prefer a backup instead of an edit? <code>kod config init-from local-fast</code> backs up your current config to <code>config.toml.bak-&lt;unix-ts&gt;</code> and writes a fresh one seeded from the profile — a one-command reset that keeps your old file.
</Aside>

## What a profile does and does not set

`profile use` writes only the model endpoint — provider, model, base URL, context window, max tokens, and generation settings. It does not touch `[memory]`, `[skills]`, `[swarm]`, `[hooks]`, `[tools]`, or `[mcp]`, and it does not create per-project overrides. Everything else stays exactly as you configured it.

## Choosing between them

A practical decision guide:

- **`local-fast`** when you are editing, asking questions, or running long interactive sessions where latency dominates. 7B models on a modern machine stream comfortably.
- **`local-capable`** when tasks are genuinely hard — multi-file refactors, subtle bug hunts — and your hardware can carry the VRAM cost.
- **`local-reasoning`** when you want deliberation over speed: DeepSeek-R1 spends more tokens thinking and less time being wrong.
- **`cloud-openai`** when quality matters more than locality and you have accepted the trade by setting `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

You can switch mid-session from the TUI with `/model <name>` — completion lists the models your server actually offers — and the switch is instantaneous because the engine does not hold the provider read lock across a streaming round.

## Beyond the presets

A profile is just a starting point. Any OpenAI-compatible server is reachable by editing the endpoint block directly — see [LLM Providers](/concepts/providers/) for how base-URL normalisation works, and [Configuration](/guides/configuration/#endpoints-instead-of-a-single-model) for the multi-endpoint shape, including routing debug tasks to a cloud model while chat stays local. The `[llm.endpoints.pricing]` table (USD per million tokens) feeds the TUI's cost display for pay-per-token endpoints.

<Aside type="note">
  Profiles target specific models, not specific providers. Pointing KOD at any other OpenAI-compatible server is a matter of setting <code>base_url</code> (and <code>model</code>) on an endpoint.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Next: Skills" href="/guides/skills/" description="Teach the agent reusable knowledge with Markdown files." />


---

---
title: Sandboxing
description: Running KOD's shell commands under OS-level containment — bwrap on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS — and why it fails loudly rather than silently.
sidebar:
  order: 9
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Sandboxing is KOD's hard containment layer for `execute_command`. Where the [policy engine](/guides/policy/) is a decision-maker, the sandbox is a wall: when `--sandbox` is active, shell commands execute through the platform's confinement primitive — **`bwrap`** (bubblewrap) on Linux or **`sandbox-exec`** on macOS — instead of directly in your session.

The design rule that makes this trustworthy: **KOD fails loudly if the primitive is unavailable rather than silently running unsandboxed.** If you asked for a sandbox and the platform cannot provide one, the command does not run and you get an error. There is no silent fallback, because a sandbox that quietly disappears is worse than no sandbox at all. The TUI also confirms it on stderr at startup (`Sandbox: required (bwrap on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS)`) so you know the flag took effect before the first shell call, not after.

## When to use it

- **Unattended runs.** Any `kod agent` invocation in a script, cron job, or pipeline should carry `--sandbox`. Combined with `--preset read-only` it gives you a run that can neither write files nor escape its process box.
- **Swarm runs.** Multiple agents executing concurrently multiply both the power and the risk; `kod swarm` plus sandboxing keeps the concurrency contained.
- **First sessions in an unfamiliar codebase.** Let the agent run tests and builds while the blast radius is bounded.

## Enabling and verifying it

<Code lang="bash" code={`# per-invocation (chat, tui, prompt, agent, swarm)
kod chat --sandbox
kod agent -g "run the test suite and fix failures" --sandbox

# confirm the primitive exists before a long unattended run
kod sandbox check`} />

`kod sandbox check` reports which primitive is available on your platform — and, when it is missing, the install command — so you can confirm support up front rather than discovering its absence mid-run.

## What the sandbox bounds

The platform primitives give the agent's shell commands a restricted filesystem view and limited network/device access. On top of that, KOD mounts `.git` read-only by default (`git.history_protected`) — the agent can read history through the git tools but cannot rewrite it from inside a sandboxed command.

What the sandbox does **not** replace:

- The policy engine still gates every tool call (allow/deny/ask, path globs, command allowlists).
- Checkpoints still snapshot files before writes, so file-level undo exists either way.
- Command allowlists (`binaries`) remain ergonomics, not guarantees — a `bash` allowlist is not containment.

<Aside type="caution">
  Sandboxing is belt-and-suspenders with the policy engine, not a substitute for it. The strongest unattended posture is all three layers: <code>--preset read-only</code>, <code>--sandbox</code>, and a committed <code>.kod/policy.toml</code> with <code>forbidden</code> globs for secrets.
</Aside>

## Platform notes

- **Linux** — bubblewrap (`bwrap`) is a small, widely packaged utility. If it is not installed, `--sandbox` errors with a clear message; install it with your distribution's package manager. `kod sandbox check` prints the exact advice.
- **macOS** — `sandbox-exec` ships with the OS (it powers App Sandbox profiles). Note that Apple marks it deprecated; it remains the available primitive today, and KOD uses it as-is.
- **Windows** — sandboxing support is limited; KOD reports the primitive as unavailable and fails loudly rather than faking it.

<LinkCard title="Reference: Tools Reference" href="/reference/tools/" description="What execute_command and every other tool can do." />


---

---
title: Sessions, Replay & Checkpoints
description: How KOD records every tool call as JSONL, how kod replay turns sessions into regression checks, and how checkpoints give you file-level undo.
sidebar:
  order: 11
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

KOD's audit story rests on three mechanisms that all live on disk, in plain formats: the **session log** (JSONL), **replay** (re-execution without the model), and **checkpoints** (file snapshots before every mutating call). Together they mean any session — yesterday's or last month's — can be reviewed, re-run, or rolled back.

## The session log

Every tool call is recorded as a JSONL entry: the tool name, its arguments, the duration, the result, and the policy decision that allowed it (`SessionEntry::PolicyDecision` carries the outcome, the rule, and the layer that produced it). Session logs are written under `~/.kod/sessions/`, named by timestamp (for example `1730000000000.jsonl`). The `KOD_SESSION_LOG` environment variable names an explicit log file when you want a stable path — a script's run, a test, an archive.

Because the format is line-delimited JSON, the log is inspectable with ordinary tools — `jq`, `grep`, `less` — no custom viewer required. It is also the substrate for `kod replay`.

Inspecting sessions from the CLI:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod sessions latest                  # path of the newest session log
kod sessions count                   # how many logs exist, combined size
kod sessions show                    # where the TUI session lives, message count
kod sessions export session.md       # TUI session as Markdown (default)
kod sessions export session.json --format json   # or JSON, for round-tripping
kod sessions import session.json     # replace the saved session (refuses malformed files)
kod sessions clear                   # delete the saved session state`} />

The TUI conversation (prompts, replies, layout state) is saved separately at `~/.kod/tui_session.json` and is what `sessions export`/`import`/`clear` operate on; the JSONL logs in `~/.kod/sessions/` are the audit trail of tool calls.

## Replay: sessions as regression checks

`kod replay <session.jsonl>` re-runs the tool calls a session made, **without the model**. Every `read_file`, `write_file`, and `execute_command` is checkable against the codebase at any later commit. This turns a historical session into a regression test: did the fix the agent made last week still hold? Does the refactoring it performed still pass?

<Code lang="bash" code={`# print what would run — always do this first
kod replay ~/.kod/sessions/1730000000000.jsonl

# actually re-execute the tool calls
kod replay ~/.kod/sessions/1730000000000.jsonl --execute`} />

<Aside type="caution">
  <code>--execute</code> performs real writes and commands against your working tree. Review the dry run first; do not pass <code>--execute</code> until you trust the session.
</Aside>

## Checkpoints: file-level undo

KOD snapshots the target file **before every mutating call** — `write_file` and `patch_file` — so the damage any single tool call can do is bounded and reversible:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod checkpoint list             # snapshots for this project, newest first (--limit 20)
kod checkpoint diff <id>        # unified diff between snapshot and current file
kod checkpoint restore <id>     # put a file back
kod checkpoint clear            # drop the checkpoint store for this project`} />

Checkpoints are per-file, not per-commit — they undo what *the agent* changed, which is usually exactly the granularity you want after a bad run. They are stored under `~/.kod/checkpoints/<project-hash>/`, keyed by your working directory, so two projects never see each other's checkpoints. `restore` does not delete the snapshot — a restore can itself be restored. Inside the TUI, `/checkpoints` lists them, `/diff` shows the most recent file diff, and `/rollback [id]` restores.

## How they compose

<Code lang="text" code={`tool call ──▶ policy decision (logged) ──▶ checkpoint snapshot ──▶ execute ──▶ result (logged)
                                                                                     │
             ◀────────────────── kod replay --execute ────────────────────────────────┘`} />

A practical audit loop: run `kod sessions latest`, read the JSONL to see what happened, replay it against a different branch or commit to see whether it still makes sense, and restore checkpoints if you want the files back the way they were.

<Aside type="note">
  This is also why the [README](https://github.com/elcoosp/kod) says “if 'where does my code go when I run this?' is a question you want a one-line answer to, KOD is for you.” The answer is: into files with checkpoints, into a JSONL log you can read, and nowhere else.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Guides: Policy & Permissions" href="/guides/policy/" description="What the PolicyDecision entries in the log mean." />


---

---
title: Skills
description: Writing and managing KOD skills — the Markdown + YAML format, the four search directories, matching rules, hot reload, and the kod skills subcommands.
sidebar:
  order: 5
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, FileTree, LinkCard, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Skills are KOD's knowledge-reuse mechanism: plain Markdown files with YAML front matter that get matched against your prompts and injected into the grounded prompt. They are how you teach the harness *your* conventions — your refactoring patterns, your testing style, your house rules — in files you can read, diff, and version like any other text.

The design goals are deliberately boring: no database, no daemon, no rebuild. A skill is a file on disk; editing it takes effect on the next prompt.

## Where skills live

KOD discovers skills in four standard directories, in order — later directories shadow earlier ones for skills that share a name:

1. `~/.kod/skills` — canonical KOD location
2. `~/.agents/skills` — Claude-style compatibility
3. `<project>/.kod/skills` — project-local KOD
4. `<project>/.agents/skills` — project-local Claude-style

Setting `skills.skills_dir` in the config replaces all of the above with a single custom directory. `kod skills` (and `/skills` in the TUI) lists the merged set from every active directory, and `kod skills --json` emits the same inventory for scripts.

## The file format

A skill is a Markdown file with YAML front matter. The parser splits the body into three sections — instructions, examples, and constraints — and all three reach the model when the skill is matched:

<Code lang="markdown" code={`---
name: rust-refactoring
description: Rust refactoring with idiomatic patterns
version: 1.0.0
category: coding
tags: [rust, refactoring, idioms]
capabilities: [code-refactoring, ownership-analysis]
triggers:
  - "refactor rust"
  - "make more idiomatic"
---

## Instructions

You are an expert Rust refactoring assistant...

## Examples

<example input="Refactor this loop">
...
</example>

## Constraints

- Never change public API without explicit request
- Preserve existing tests`} />

What each part does:

- **`triggers`** — phrases that should activate the skill. Matching considers triggers, tags, capabilities, and the name, scored against a threshold (`skills.match_threshold`, default 0.7); the [Task Router](/concepts/router/) decides which skills ride along with a prompt.
- **`tags` and `capabilities`** — coarser activation signals, useful when a skill should attach to a *kind* of task rather than a phrase.
- **Instructions** — the operating guidance injected into the prompt.
- **Examples** — concrete input/output demonstrations; they cost tokens but sharpen behaviour.
- **Constraints** — hard rules the model is asked to respect. Put your non-negotiables here.

## Managing skills from the CLI

The `kod skills` subcommand tree is a small skill package manager:

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod skills                       # list (same as \`kod skills list\`)
kod skills new my-skill          # scaffold in the first writable dir
kod skills show my-skill         # full markdown content
kod skills source my-skill       # absolute path of the file
kod skills edit my-skill         # open in $EDITOR
kod skills search "refactor"     # search names, descriptions, tags
kod skills rename my-skill my-skill-v2
kod skills copy my-skill other-name
kod skills export my-skill -     # write to stdout / a path
kod skills remove my-skill       # refuses without --yes outside cwd`} />

`new` refuses to overwrite an existing file, `rename`/`copy` rewrite the `name:` field inside the file so the front matter never drifts, and `remove` asks for `--yes` unless the target is inside the current directory. For CI, `kod validate-skills` exits non-zero on malformed skills — and `kod validate-skills-strict` also fails skills that omit a `version` — so broken front matter fails your pipeline instead of silently not matching.

<Aside type="tip">
  Hot reload is on by default (<code>skills.enable_hot_reload</code>). Keep a project skill open in one pane, edit it, and the next prompt in the other pane sees the change — the fastest loop for tuning triggers and constraints.
</Aside>

## A practical first skill

<Steps>
1. Scaffold it:

   <Code lang="bash" code={`kod skills new python-testing`} />

2. Edit the front matter — give it two or three triggers that match how you actually ask for the task.
3. Write **constraints** first (the rules that must never be broken), then instructions, then one small example.
4. Verify it matches:

   <Code lang="bash" code={`kod skills search "testing"`} />
</Steps>

Examples of the format — including `python-testing` and `code-review` — ship in the repository under `skills/examples/`.

<FileTree>
- ~/.kod/skills/
  - rust-refactoring.md
  - python-testing.md
  - code-review.md
- my-project/.kod/skills/
  - house-style.md
</FileTree>

<Aside type="note">
  If a skill never seems to fire, check what the matcher sees: <code>kod skills show &lt;name&gt;</code> prints the file as parsed, and <code>kod skills search "&lt;words from your prompt&gt;"</code> tells you whether the trigger text overlaps at all. Both are covered in the [FAQ](/guides/faq/#why-is-my-skill-never-matched).
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Reference: Skill File Format" href="/reference/skill-format/" description="The exact front matter schema, section parsing rules, and shadowing order." />


---

---
title: Agent Swarms
description: kod swarm — decomposing a goal into subtasks, running up to 8 agents concurrently, detecting file conflicts, and merging the results.
sidebar:
  order: 10
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A swarm is KOD's answer to “this task is too big for one pass.” `kod swarm` decomposes a goal into N subtasks, spawns N agents, runs them **concurrently** against a shared workspace, detects file conflicts between them, and asks the model to merge the per-agent results into a single answer.

## The lifecycle

<Steps>
1. **Decompose** — the runner asks the model to break your goal into subtasks, targeting `swarm.max_agents` pieces.
2. **Spawn** — up to N agents start with their own subtask. The runner clamps N to the range **2–8**: a one-agent swarm is not a swarm, and eight concurrent agentic loops will saturate most local model servers.
3. **Run** — agents loop independently (classify → ground → stream → tools), coordinated through a communication hub with a shared workspace and per-path locks. They share findings through the `swarm_note` / `swarm_read` blackboard tools.
4. **Detect conflicts** — file-level locks and a conflict resolver surface agents that touched the same paths.
5. **Merge** — when `swarm.merge_results` is true (the default), the model synthesizes one final answer from the per-agent results. When false — or when synthesis fails — the results are concatenated under their labels.
</Steps>

## Running one

<Code lang="bash" code={`kod swarm -g "implement and test a rate limiter for the HTTP client" -n 4`} />

Flags that matter: `-n, --agents` overrides the configured agent count (still clamped to 2–8) and `--model` switches the model for the whole run. Inside the TUI, `/swarm <goal>` starts the same flow interactively. Disabling result merging is a config decision, not a flag: set `swarm.merge_results = false` in `config.toml` to always get labeled per-agent output.

<Aside type="tip">
  Swarms shine when subtasks are <em>file-disjoint</em> — “module A”, “module B”, “tests”. You get real parallelism and no merge conflicts. When subtasks must touch the same files, prefer a single <code>kod agent</code> run or keep <code>-n</code> small.
</Aside>

## Configuration

<Code lang="toml" code={`[swarm]
max_agents         = 5     # the decompose step targets this; runner clamps to 2–8
merge_results      = true  # false = concatenate per-agent results under labels
agent_timeout_secs = 300   # per-agent wall clock; a stuck agent is cancelled; 0 disables
agent_retries      = 1     # extra attempts after a timeout or provider error`} />

The config section is minimal on purpose — it carries only the values the swarm runner actually consumes. Coordination strategy and lock timeouts are not tunable because they are not parameters worth exposing; the defaults encode one opinionated pipeline.

## Routing swarm roles to different models

If your config defines multiple endpoints, `[llm.routing].swarm` maps swarm capabilities to endpoints — the same multi-model routing that `by_task` provides for ordinary prompts:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[llm.routing.swarm]
Planning = "cloud"   # the decompose/merge step thinks with the bigger model
Coding   = "local"   # the per-agent implementation work stays local`} />

See [Configuration](/guides/configuration/#endpoints-instead-of-a-single-model) for the endpoint blocks these names refer to.

## Shared workspace and safety

The workspace coordinator keeps agents from stomping each other through two mechanisms:

1. **Per-path advisory locks** — the same table the tool layer uses for concurrent writes; two agents cannot silently interleave writes to the same file.
2. **Conflict detection + resolution** — when agents do contend for the same paths, the conflicts are detected and reported rather than resolved by last-write-wins.

Policy applies per agent: every agent's tool calls go through the same [policy engine](/guides/policy/) as single-agent runs. `--sandbox` (on `kod swarm` like `kod agent`) confines every agent's shell commands, and `--preset read-only` turns a swarm into a read-only analysis crew.

<Aside type="caution">
  A swarm with <code>yolo</code> and no sandbox multiplies unsupervised write access by N. For unattended runs, the safe posture is <code>--preset read-only</code> plus <code>--sandbox</code>, or a strict <code>.kod/policy.toml</code>.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Concepts: The Agent Loop" href="/concepts/agent-loop/" description="What each swarm agent is doing per round." />


---

---
title: Telemetry
description: Export turn- and tool-level records to an OpenTelemetry collector. Off unless you set an endpoint.
sidebar:
  order: 16
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

KOD can export structured records to an OpenTelemetry collector. It is **off by default and costs nothing when off** — the handle is constructed from the environment, and an unset endpoint yields a disabled no-op that every record call short-circuits on.

## Turning it on

Set the standard OTLP environment variable before starting `kod`:

<Code lang="bash" code={`export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="http://localhost:4317"
kod tui`} />

Startup prints one line confirming the export, including the service name:

<Code lang="ansi" code={`kod: OTLP telemetry enabled (service.name="kod")`} />

`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is the only switch. There is no config-file key — telemetry is operator infrastructure, not agent behaviour, so it lives entirely in the environment where a deployment can set it without touching a project's `.kod/`.

## What is exported

| Record | When |
| --- | --- |
| turn | once per completed turn: model, token usage, duration, outcome |
| tool | once per tool call: tool name, duration, success or failure |

Prompt and completion **content** is not exported. The records describe the shape of a session — which tools ran, how long a turn took, how many tokens it cost — not what was said.

<Aside type="caution">
  Tool arguments are not included either, but tool *names* are. A custom tool whose name encodes a secret would leak it through the record; do not name tools after their inputs.
</Aside>

## When it is off

`Telemetry::from_env()` returns a disabled handle. Every `record_*` method is a no-op, no exporter is constructed, and no background task is spawned. A session that never set the endpoint pays nothing for the feature existing.

## Related

- [Cost and limits](/reference/config/#limits) — the session's own budget accounting, which is separate from what telemetry exports.
- [Tracing](/guides/troubleshooting/) — the local turn-trace file (`kod trace`), useful when you want records without a collector.


---

---
title: Tools
description: What KOD's built-in tools can do — file system, git, shell, project checks, memory, LSP, and web — and how every call is permission-gated, path-locked, and sandboxed.
sidebar:
  order: 7
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Tools are how the agent touches your system. KOD ships 24 built-in tools, and every single call passes through the same gauntlet: the [policy engine](/guides/policy/) decides allow/deny/ask, the executor enforces a timeout, a per-path advisory lock table prevents concurrent writes to the same file, and `--sandbox` can route shell commands through the platform sandbox. `kod tools list` prints the registry exactly as the model sees it; `kod tools show <name>` prints one tool's schema.

## The tool families

**File system** — `read_file`, `write_file`, `patch_file`, `list_files`, `grep`, `file_info`, `search_files`. The write paths are careful: `write_file` results attach a unified diff of what changed, and both `write_file` and `patch_file` snapshot the target file first so [checkpoints](/guides/sessions/#checkpoints-file-level-undo) can restore it. `search_files` finds files by name pattern when `grep`'s content search is the wrong shape.

**Git** — `git_status`, `git_diff`, `git_commit`, `git_branch`. Status and diff are read-only; commit and branch-create are write-gated like any other mutating tool. Together they let the agent reason about your working tree and — when policy allows — commit its own work on a branch without shelling out.

**Shell** — `execute_command`, the most powerful and the most gated tool. It is the one most affected by policy presets (denied outright under `read-only`), command allowlists (`binaries` / `forbidden_binaries` in `.kod/policy.toml`), and sandboxing.

**Project checks** — `check` runs the compiler or linter that matches your project — Cargo, `tsc`, `ruff`, or `go vet` — and returns structured diagnostics. The agent uses it to ask "did that edit break the build?" without grepping compiler output.

**Planning and interaction** — `todo` maintains a visible task list for multi-step work, and `ask_user` lets the agent stop and ask *you* a question instead of guessing.

**Memory** — `memory_save` and `memory_search` give the model direct access to the long-term store. Registered only when memory is enabled; see [Memory](/guides/memory/).

**Swarm** — `swarm_note` and `swarm_read`, a shared blackboard that concurrent agents use to publish and read each other's findings; see [Agent Swarms](/guides/swarm/).

**Web** — `web_fetch`, an HTTP/HTTPS fetch with SSRF protection: loopback, private, link-local, and metadata endpoints are refused. It is the only tool that can reach the network, and only when `llm.network_access` (or the tool's own `network` policy) enables it.

**LSP** — `lsp_diagnostics`, `lsp_definition`, `lsp_references`, `lsp_hover`. When a language server for the file's language is on your `PATH`, these give the agent compiler-grade answers — otherwise they fail with a message naming the missing server. See below.

## Permission gating in one paragraph

There is no ungated path. The `Tool` trait's execution context (`ToolContext`) carries permissions and anchors relative paths to a working directory; the policy engine consults the effective policy — preset, global config, project `.kod/policy.toml`, CLI override — before every call, and the decision (including which rule and which layer decided) is logged to the session. A `deny` always wins over an `allow` at glob-conflict time, and path globs follow gitignore semantics: `*` does not cross `/`, `**` does.

## Concurrency safety

A per-path advisory lock table means two agents (say, in a [swarm](/guides/swarm/)) cannot silently interleave writes to the same file. Conflicts are detected and surfaced rather than last-write-wins. This is what makes the swarm's shared-workspace mode usable instead of terrifying.

## Which tool when

| You want the agent to… | Tool that runs | Typical policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inspect code, find patterns | `read_file`, `list_files`, `grep`, `file_info`, `search_files` | allowed everywhere |
| Edit a file | `write_file` / `patch_file` | `ask` under `standard` |
| Understand recent changes | `git_status`, `git_diff` | allowed |
| Commit work / create a branch | `git_commit`, `git_branch` | `ask` under `standard` |
| Run tests, build, format | `execute_command` | `ask` under `standard` |
| Verify the build after an edit | `check` | allowed (read-only by nature) |
| Look something up online | `web_fetch` | needs network access enabled |
| Save a fact for later | `memory_save` / `memory_search` | allowed when memory is on |

## Write follow-ups: LSP and check

Two config switches add automatic verification after every successful write:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[tools]
auto_lsp   = true    # default — cheap, sub-second per file
auto_check = false   # opt-in — runs the compiler, which is not free`} />

- **`auto_lsp`** runs the language server's diagnostics pass on the touched files and appends a `## LSP diagnostics` block to the next turn's prompt. It only runs for languages that have a server on `PATH`; a session with none installed simply sees no block. The same capability is available to the agent on demand via `lsp_diagnostics`, `lsp_definition`, `lsp_references`, and `lsp_hover`.
- **`auto_check`** runs the project check (`cargo`, `tsc`, `ruff`, `go vet`) and appends its diagnostics the same way. A baseline is captured at startup, so the model is shown *its* errors, not pre-existing ones. On a large workspace this adds a compiler run per write — that is why it defaults to off. The TUI's `/check` runs the same check on demand.

<Aside type="note">
  Where a language server is missing, the LSP tools do not silently return nothing — they error with a message naming the missing binary, and the model can tell you what to install.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Reference: Tools Reference" href="/reference/tools/" description="Every tool's arguments, result shape, and gating in one table." />


---

---
title: Troubleshooting
description: Common KOD problems and fixes — endpoint issues, config trouble, memory errors, permission confusion, and what kod doctor tells you.
sidebar:
  order: 13
type: how-to
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Most KOD problems have short causes: a model server that is not running, a config typo, a policy rule doing exactly what you asked it to do. This page collects the frequent ones, in the order you are likely to meet them. For question-shaped problems (“where are my sessions?”, “how do I reset X?”), see the [FAQ](/guides/faq/).

## Start with `kod doctor`

`kod doctor` is the triage tool. It checks the config file, the model endpoint, discovered skills, the memory database, the sandbox primitive, and git availability, and prints a verdict for each. Run it before anything else; half of the entries below are “doctor would have told you.” `kod doctor --fix` creates missing directories and writes a default config if none exists — it never touches an existing config.

## The endpoint is not reachable

**Symptom:** the first prompt hangs and then fails; `kod doctor` marks the endpoint check failed.

**Fixes, in order of likelihood:**

1. The model server is not running. Start it — `ollama serve` — or start LM Studio's server / MLX Omni Serve / vLLM.
2. Wrong base URL. Ollama's OpenAI-compatible root is `http://localhost:11434/v1`; the default config points there. `kod profile show` prints the effective `[llm]` block so you can see what KOD actually uses.
3. The model name does not exist on the server. `kod models` lists what the provider offers (`--filter` narrows). Note the server's model name is what counts (`qwen2.5-coder:7b`), not the profile name.
4. A cloud endpoint returns 401. `api_key_env` names the environment variable that must hold the key — check the variable is set *in the shell you launched KOD from*.

## Config problems

**Symptom:** warnings at startup, or values not behaving as you expect.

- Out-of-range values (temperature, context window, max tokens, timeout) are **clamped with a warning at load time** — read the warning; it names the endpoint and the corrected value.
- A corrupt config file does not brick anything: KOD warns and falls back to defaults. `kod config validate` exits non-zero on invalid TOML, which makes it easy to check a hand-edit before starting a session.
- To see *effective* configuration rather than the raw file, `kod config show-merged` prints defaults merged with your settings — self-documenting and reproducible.
- Old keys are silently ignored rather than erroring — if a `[llm]` block from an older example seems to do nothing, rewrite it as an `[[llm.endpoints]]` block (see [Configuration](/guides/configuration/)).

## “The agent refused to write / run anything”

That is the [policy engine](/guides/policy/) working as configured:

- **`read-only` preset** denies `write_file`, `patch_file`, and `execute_command` without asking. If you launched with `--preset read-only`, that is why. Unset it or use `standard`.
- **`.kod/policy.toml`** in the project root may deny a path (`forbidden` globs) or a binary (`forbidden_binaries`). The decision is logged with its rule and source layer — check the session log entry, or run `kod policy explain <tool> <args>` to see the verdict without a session.
- **`standard` preset with nobody to approve**: `kod agent` and `kod prompt` cannot answer approval prompts, so approved-required calls are refused immediately with a message. For scripts, prefer an explicit `--preset read-only` run design.

## Memory errors

**Symptom:** the long-term store errors on open.

- A stale or corrupt `redb` file is fixed by deleting it — it lives at `~/.kod/data/kod.redb` (global scope) or `<cwd>/.kod/memory.redb` (project scope), and it will be recreated on next use. Your sessions and checkpoints are stored elsewhere and survive.
- `kod memory clear` empties entries without touching the file itself.

## TUI state trouble

**Symptom:** the TUI reopens a conversation you wanted gone, or a corrupt state file breaks startup.

- The TUI resumes from `~/.kod/tui_session.json` (directory overridable with `KOD_TUI_STATE_DIR`). `kod sessions clear` removes it deliberately.
- If the state file is corrupt, delete it — history and sessions on disk are unaffected. Note that `kod tui --no-resume` currently prints a hint rather than skipping the file; moving the file aside is the reliable fresh start.

## Where to look next

- `kod sessions latest` + the JSONL log — what actually happened, including every policy decision with its source.
- `kod tools list` — what the model can actually call right now (MCP and LSP tools appear here when available).
- `kod skills` — whether the skills you expect are actually loaded and matched (`--json` for scripts).
- `kod map` — what the engine can see of your repository; surprising answers often trace to a surprising repo map.

<Aside type="note">
  If a fix here does not cover it, the [CONTRIBUTING guide](/developers/contributing/) explains what to include in a bug report — session log excerpts make reports dramatically easier to act on.
</Aside>


---

---
title: Terminal UI (TUI)
description: Living in the KOD TUI — layout, modes, tool rows, search, themes, slash commands, completions, and the context meter.
sidebar:
  order: 1
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The TUI is KOD's primary interface: a ratatui-based terminal application with a chat area, live tool rows, an agent panel, type-ahead search, themes, and slash commands. It talks to the same engine as the CLI, so everything it does — session logging, policy decisions, memory updates — behaves identically to `kod chat`. The difference is comfort: the TUI is built for long, interactive sessions where you inspect what the agent is doing while it does it.

Launch it with `kod tui`. Flags you will actually use: `--model <name>` to start with a different model, `--preset read-only` to lock the session down, and `--sandbox` to confine shell commands.

## The layout

Four regions divide the screen:

- **Header** — the session state, the loaded model, and the active policy preset.
- **Chat area** — your prompts, the assistant's streaming replies, and one row per tool call. Tool rows render live as the agent works: tool name, target path or command, and a ✓/✗ outcome.
- **Status line** — mode indicator (normal/insert), the context meter, and other session vitals.
- **Input box** — the prompt editor, with history, completions, and multi-line editing.

Tool rows are collapsed by default so the transcript stays readable. This is a deliberate trade: you get a clean narrative view, and every tool call is still one keystroke away.

## Modes and movement

The TUI is modal. **Normal mode** is for navigation and commands; **insert mode** is for typing prompts. Press `i` to enter insert mode and `Esc` to return to normal mode — and note that `Esc` in normal mode cancels a running generation.

Scrolling and search work in normal mode: `j`/`k` move line by line, `g`/`G` jump to the oldest/newest message, `PgUp`/`PgDn` page, and `f` opens a type-ahead search with `n`/`N` cycling matches. `/grep <regex>` searches the transcript with a regular expression instead. `y` copies the last assistant reply to the clipboard, and `?` opens the help overlay if you lose track.

## Tool rows and transparency

Every tool call the agent makes renders as its own row. Expanding a row (`o` for the newest collapsed row, `t` to toggle all) shows the arguments and the result — including unified diffs attached to `write_file` and `patch_file` results. Watching diffs appear inline is the fastest way to build trust in a run: you see exactly what changed, character by character, before you ever look at git.

When a write lands, KOD can follow up automatically: with `tools.auto_lsp = true` (the default) a language-server diagnostics pass runs on the touched file and its findings are appended to the next prompt; with `tools.auto_check = true` the project's compiler or linter runs too. See [Tools](/guides/tools/#write-follow-ups-lsp-and-check).

<Aside type="tip">
  If you only learn one keybinding, learn <code>t</code>. Toggling tool-output visibility lets you flip between “narrative” and “full forensics” views of the same session.
</Aside>

## Steering, cancelling, retrying

While a generation runs you have three options, all non-destructive:

1. **Steer** — type a plain prompt. It is queued and delivered to the model as guidance; the work already done is kept. This is identical to `/steer` and is usually the right move.
2. **Cancel** — `Esc` (normal mode) or `/cancel`. The round stops; completed tool results stay in the session.
3. **Wait** — the tool loop caps itself at 40 tool rounds per prompt, so no run is infinite.

After the fact, `/retry` resends the last prompt, `e` edits your last message before resending — faster than re-typing a long instruction — and `/regenerate` asks for a fresh reply without resending your prompt.

## Slash commands

Typing `/` in insert mode opens a completion popup; `Tab` cycles it. There are around fifty built-in commands — the complete, annotated table lives at [TUI Keybindings](/reference/tui-keys/#slash-commands). They group into a few families:

- **Conversation**: `/clear`, `/undo`, `/compact`, `/summarize`, `/edit`, `/retry`, `/regenerate`, `/delete`, `/branch`, `/fork`, `/handoff`
- **Model and tools**: `/model`, `/skills`, `/tools`, `/goal`, `/system`, `/map`, `/check`, `/git-status`
- **Files and history**: `/attach`, `/diff`, `/rollback`, `/checkpoints`, `/export`, `/save`, `/load`
- **Memory**: `/memory [search|delete|clear]` — the long-term store, without leaving the chat
- **Introspection**: `/context`, `/stats`, `/whoami`, `/debug last-prompt`, `/log`
- **Housekeeping**: `/theme`, `/search`, `/grep`, `/copy`, `/raw`, `/pin`, `/unpin`, `/reset`, `/doctor`, `/init`, `/help`, `/swarm`, `/quit`, `/clearall`

Three deserve a call-out:

- `/compact` summarises the conversation to reclaim context-window headroom; `/pin <n>` protects a message from being compacted away, and `/context` shows where the window is going.
- `/fork [label]` saves the current chat as a restorable fork — cheap insurance before a risky prompt. `/branch` drops a labelled marker into the transcript instead.
- `/handoff` writes a handoff document and starts a fresh session with it as context — the clean way to end a long session and pick up tomorrow.

`/clearall` is the scorched-earth option: chat, long-term memory, *and* checkpoints for this project, behind a confirmation.

## Custom slash commands

Anything you put in a `[commands]` block in `config.toml` becomes a slash command:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[commands]
review = "Review the last change in {cwd} and point out risks."
explain = "Explain what this code does:\\n\\n{args}"`} />

`/review` sends the first template verbatim; `/explain <selection>` replaces `{args}` with everything you typed after the command name, and `{cwd}` with the working directory. Custom commands appear in the completion popup alongside the built-ins.

## Themes

The TUI ships `dark` and `light` themes, selected with `/theme [dark|light]` or `theme = "light"` in a `theme.toml` next to the config. A full custom `[theme]` table in that file overrides individual colors (the palette accepts the same color names ratatui does: `black`, `red`, `green`, …), so you can match your terminal colorscheme exactly. `kod theme list` prints the built-ins and `kod theme show dark` dumps a palette as JSON — handy when writing your own.

## Completions, history, and the mouse

In insert mode, `Tab` cycles completions for slash commands, model names (after `/model `), and file paths. `Up`/`Down` walk the history directly, and the draft you were typing is stashed — `Down` past the newest entry brings it back. Line editing follows the usual conventions — `Ctrl+W` deletes a word, `Ctrl+U` clears the line, `Ctrl+K` kills to the end, `Ctrl+Left`/`Ctrl+Right` jump by word — and `Ctrl+J` (or `Shift+Enter`) inserts a newline without sending.

The mouse works too: the wheel scrolls the chat, and `Option`/`Shift`+drag selects text the normal way.

<Aside type="note">
  The TUI resumes where you left off: the session is saved to <code>~/.kod/tui_session.json</code> (override the directory with <code>KOD_TUI_STATE_DIR</code>) and prompt history to <code>tui_history.json</code> next to it. To start deliberately fresh, move those files aside — or point <code>KOD_TUI_STATE_DIR</code> at an empty directory.
</Aside>

<LinkCard title="Reference: TUI Keybindings" href="/reference/tui-keys/" description="Every keybinding and slash command in one table." />

## One binary. Every model you already run.

KOD ships as a single Rust executable that runs the agent loop, the tools, the memory store, and the terminal UI. There is no Node runtime, no Python interpreter, and no Docker daemon in the path — just `cargo build --release` and a model server you control.

<div class="kod-stats not-content" role="list">
  <div class="stat" role="listitem"><span class="num">1</span><span class="lbl">binary to build, nothing else to install</span></div>
  <div class="stat" role="listitem"><span class="num">27</span><span class="lbl">built-in, permission-gated tools</span></div>
  <div class="stat" role="listitem"><span class="num">4</span><span class="lbl">model profiles ready out of the box</span></div>
  <div class="stat" role="listitem"><span class="num">0</span><span class="lbl">bytes of code uploaded by default</span></div>
</div>

<div class="landing-section">

## Built for people who read their own diffs

KOD is designed around one question: *where does my code go when I run this?* Every design decision — from the local model default to the JSONL session log — exists so that the answer is always “nowhere you did not choose.”

<div class="kod-features not-content">

<div class="feat">
  <span class="icon"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M12 2 3 6v6c0 5 4 8.4 9 10 5-1.6 9-5 9-10V6l-9-4Z"/><path d="m9 12 2 2 4-5"/></svg></span>
  <h3>Policy before every tool call</h3>
  <p>Read-only, standard, or yolo presets, layered with a committed <code>.kod/policy.toml</code>: per-tool allow/deny/ask, path globs, and command allowlists. Deny always wins.</p>
</div>

<div class="feat">
  <span class="icon"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M2 12s3.5-7 10-7 10 7 10 7-3.5 7-10 7-10-7-10-7Z"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="3"/></svg></span>
  <h3>Auditable by design</h3>
  <p>Every tool call is recorded as JSONL. <code>kod replay</code> re-runs a session's tool calls without the model, so you can verify any session against the codebase at any later commit.</p>
</div>

<div class="feat">
  <span class="icon"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M4 19.5A2.5 2.5 0 0 1 6.5 17H20"/><path d="M6.5 2H20v20H6.5A2.5 2.5 0 0 1 4 19.5v-15A2.5 2.5 0 0 1 6.5 2Z"/></svg></span>
  <h3>Markdown skills, hot-reloaded</h3>
  <p>Drop a Markdown file with YAML front matter into <code>~/.kod/skills</code> and the next prompt sees it. Triggers, tags, capabilities, and examples — no rebuild, no restart.</p>
</div>

<div class="feat">
  <span class="icon"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><ellipse cx="12" cy="5" rx="8" ry="3"/><path d="M4 5v6c0 1.7 3.6 3 8 3s8-1.3 8-3V5"/><path d="M4 11v6c0 1.7 3.6 3 8 3s8-1.3 8-3v-6"/></svg></span>
  <h3>Layered memory on disk</h3>
  <p>Short-term FIFO context plus a persistent <code>redb</code> long-term store — global or project-scoped. Browse it with <code>kod memory</code>, export it, or delete it.</p>
</div>

<div class="feat">
  <span class="icon"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="6" cy="6" r="3"/><circle cx="18" cy="6" r="3"/><circle cx="12" cy="18" r="3"/><path d="M8.4 7.8 10.5 15M15.6 7.8 13.5 15M9 6h6"/></svg></span>
  <h3>Agent swarms</h3>
  <p><code>kod swarm</code> decomposes a goal into subtasks, runs up to 8 agents concurrently, detects file conflicts, and asks the model to merge the results.</p>

  <h3>Optional sandboxing</h3>
  <p><code>--sandbox</code> routes shell commands through <code>bwrap</code> on Linux or <code>sandbox-exec</code> on macOS — and fails loudly if the primitive is missing, rather than running unsandboxed.</p>

## Up and running in five commands

<Tabs>
<TabItem label="Build from source">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`git clone https://github.com/elcoosp/kod.git
cd kod && cargo build --release

ollama serve &                 # or LM Studio, MLX, vLLM, …
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

./target/release/kod doctor
./target/release/kod profile use local-fast
./target/release/kod tui`} />
</TabItem>
<TabItem label="Try the CLI first">
  <Code lang="bash" code={`# one-shot agent run against a goal
kod agent -g "add a doc comment to every public function in src/lib.rs"

# a single non-interactive prompt, ideal for scripts
kod prompt "explain what src/net.rs does in three bullets"

# a swarm of 4 agents on something bigger
kod swarm -g "implement and test a rate limiter" -n 4

# replay a recorded session as a regression check
kod replay ~/.kod/sessions/1730000000000.jsonl --execute`} />
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

<Aside type="tip">
  Not sure whether your setup works? <code>kod doctor</code> prints a diagnostics report for config, endpoint, skills, memory, sandbox, and git in one shot.
</Aside>
